Gemini said
I've reviewed your config.py file. It is well-structured for a FastAPI/Pydantic backend, but there are a few critical adjustments needed to resolve the "Service Unavailable" and authentication issues we've been seeing in your console.
The "Extra Field" Crash (Critical Fix)
In your SettingsConfigDict, you are missing the instruction to ignore extra variables found in your .env file. Since your .env contains keys like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and MAPBOX_ACCESS_TOKEN, Pydantic will crash if they aren't explicitly defined in the class.
Change this:
Python
model_config = SettingsConfigDict( env_file=".env", env_file_encoding="utf-8", case_sensitive=False, )
To this:
Python
model_config = SettingsConfigDict( env_file=".env", env_file_encoding="utf-8", case_sensitive=False, extra="ignore", # This prevents the app from crashing on extra .env variables )
Vertex AI Variable Names
Your Settings class uses lowercase names like vertex_ai_project and google_application_credentials. While Pydantic's case_sensitive=False usually handles this, it is safer to match the exact uppercase names used in your .env.
Project ID: Ensure your .env has VERTEX_AI_PROJECT="blissful-jet-489205-b8".
Credentials: Ensure your .env has GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS="vertex-key.json".
Verification of Pre-loading Logic
The logic at the top of your file that manually injects the credentials into os.environ is excellent:
Python
_dotenv = dotenv_values(Path(file).resolve().parent.parent.parent / ".env") if _gac := _dotenv.get("GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS"): os.environ.setdefault("GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS", _gac)
This ensures that Google's authentication library finds your vertex-key.json file the moment the server starts.
Summary of Observations
Location: Your default location is set to northamerica-northeast1, which is perfect for your Calgary-based project.
Model: You are correctly targeting imagen-3.0-capability-001.
Database: Your URL normalization logic is already set up to handle the postgresql+asyncpg format required for your spatial data.
Recommendation: Apply the extra="ignore" fix to config.py, restart your backend server on port 5174, and try the "Site Plan" render again. That should finally clear the 503 error.

Where the gap is
The main quality gap is that this reference likely uses pre-rendered 3D models composited onto the aerial photo, not a diffusion model. Imagen 3 inpainting won't produce that level of geometric precision (perfectly straight glass curtain walls, accurate window grids, correct perspective foreshortening) in a single pass.
To close that gap, the highest-impact next steps would be:
Higher guidance_scale (20+) to force stricter prompt adherence
Per-zone sequential rendering at higher zoom for better architectural detail
Richer archetype negative prompts to suppress distortion and cartoon artifacts
Iterative refinement — render → upscale → re-inpaint to sharpen details

Post-processing function being added:
def _post_process(image_b64: str) -> str:
    raw = base64.b64decode(image_b64)
    img = Image.open(io.BytesIO(raw)).convert("RGB")
    img = ImageEnhance.Sharpness(img).enhance(1.12)
    img = ImageEnhance.Contrast(img).enhance(1.03)
    img = ImageEnhance.Color(img).enhance(1.04)
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    img.save(buf, format="PNG")
    return base64.b64encode(buf.getvalue()).decode()

Modified handleSave to resolve shade color from archetype and include in update:
const handleSave = () => {
  const archetypeId = (props.development_archetype_id as string)
    || (props.road_archetype_id as string)
    || (props.green_space_archetype_id as string)
    || (props.plaza_archetype_id as string);
  const shadeColor = archetypeId ? getShadeForArchetype(archetypeId) : undefined;
  onUpdate(zone.id, {
    name: name || undefined,
    color: shadeColor !== '#888888' ? shadeColor : undefined,
    properties: props,
  });
};

Clean. Here's what I fixed:
Fix 1 — Stitching winding-rule bug: stitchWithBoundaryMask() was building a combined clip path from ALL zone polygons. When inner zones had opposite winding from the site boundary, the canvas nonzero fill rule subtracted them, creating holes — so the AI result only showed in gaps between zones, while colored overlays remained visible inside zone polygons. Now it clips only to the site boundary (the master container), so the full AI render shows across the entire site.
Fix 2 — Prompt deduplication: Multiple zones sharing the same default color (e.g., two road zones both #616161) were merged into a single prompt entry. Now deduplicates by color + zoneType to preserve distinct zone types.
These two fixes should ensure all zones get fully replaced by the AI render, matching the Richmond reference quality. Try another render and let me know how it looks.

That's a coordinate mapping bug in renderPerZone. When the function zooms into each zone and gets the AI render back, it tries to composite the zoomed render onto the original full-view image — but the pixel coordinates don't match because the map viewport changed.
The fix: don't zoom in. Keep the map at the original viewport and render each zone with its own mask and prompt, but from the same camera position. This gives the prompt differentiation benefit without coordinate mismatch.

Key Technical Concepts:
Google Vertex AI Imagen 3 — imagen-3.0-capability-001 model for editing/inpainting
EDIT_MODE_INPAINT_INSERTION — paints only inside white mask pixels
Binary mask: white (255) = edit area, black (0) = keep untouched
Unique Shade ID system — 73 archetypes mapped to unique hex colors within hue families (red for commercial, yellow for residential, gray for streets)
Canvas nonzero winding rule — caused clip path holes when inner zone polygons had opposite winding from site boundary
DPR (devicePixelRatio) rounding — ±1px differences between mask and image dimensions caused by async timing between toBlob() and generateBinaryMask()
Per-zone sequential rendering — render each zone individually with zone-specific mask and prompt, then composite
Structured 3-block prompt — Block 1 (Anchor Command), Block 2 (Zone Mapping), Block 3 (Environmental Context)
Stitching/compositing — clip AI render to zone polygons and overlay on original satellite image
map.project() — converts geographic coordinates to CSS pixel coordinates (NOT device pixels)

Change 1e: Dynamic colorName — Replaced hardcoded color→name map with archetype-aware lookup:
import { getArchetypeForShade } from '@/data/archetypeShadeMap';

function colorName(hex: string): string {
  const archetypeId = getArchetypeForShade(hex);
  if (archetypeId) {
    const entry = catalog?.find((a: any) => a.id === archetypeId || archetypeId.startsWith(a.id + '_'));
    if (entry?.title) return `${entry.title} shade (${hex})`;
  }
  const genericMap: Record<string, string> = { /* existing mappings */ };
  return genericMap[hex] || hex;
}
Stitching fix — Changed stitchWithBoundaryMask to clip only to site_boundary:
const boundaries = siteZones.filter(z => z.zone_type === 'site_boundary' && z.coordinates && z.coordinates.length >= 3);
const clipZones = boundaries.length > 0 ? boundaries : siteZones.filter(z => z.coordinates && z.coordinates.length >= 3);
ctx.save();
ctx.beginPath();
for (const zone of clipZones) {
  const pixels = siteBoundaryToPixels(map, zone.coordinates!);
  ctx.moveTo(pixels[0].x * dpr, pixels[0].y * dpr);
  for (let i = 1; i < pixels.length; i++) {
    ctx.lineTo(pixels[i].x * dpr, pixels[i].y * dpr);
  }
  ctx.closePath();
}
ctx.clip();
Deduplication fix — Changed from color-only to color+zoneType:
const seen = new Map<string, ZonePromptEntry>();
for (const entry of entries) {
  const key = `${entry.color}_${entry.zoneType}`;
  if (!seen.has(key)) {
    seen.set(key, entry);
  } else if (entry.archetypeTitle && !seen.get(key)!.archetypeTitle) {
    seen.set(key, entry);
  }
}
// Sort: buildings/parks first, site_boundary LAST
const result = Array.from(seen.values());
result.sort((a, b) => {
  if (a.zoneType === 'site_boundary') return 1;
  if (b.zoneType === 'site_boundary') return -1;
  return 0;
});
return result;

    if raw_img.size != mask_img.size:

Here's what I changed and why:
Root cause hypothesis: The hardcoded '4:3' aspect ratio was being sent to Vertex AI for all renders, but your map canvas likely isn't 4:3. Vertex AI's editing API may resize/crop the output to match the requested aspect ratio, causing the rendered content to be offset or scaled differently than the input — making it look like "nothing rendered" when composited back.
Fixes applied:
Dynamic aspect ratio (computeAspectRatio) — now computes the closest standard ratio (1:1, 3:4, 4:3, 9:16, 16:9) from the actual map canvas dimensions. All renderSingle and per-zone callVertexAI calls now use this instead of hardcoded 4:3.
Comprehensive debug logging added to the per-zone pipeline:
Mask coverage: White pixel count and percentage logged from generateSingleZoneMask — if this is 0%, the mask is all-black and the AI has nothing to edit
Prompt text: Full prompt logged for each zone so you can verify it's correct
Aspect ratio: Logged so you can see what's being sent
Compositing coordinates: Clip polygon pixel coordinates logged so you can verify they're within the canvas bounds
Backend dimension check: Input vs output image dimensions logged to detect any resize by Vertex AI

This console log is the "smoking gun." It confirms that your application is trying to call an experimental model (gemini-2.0-flash-exp) that has likely been retired or moved to a different API version in this March 2026 environment.
The 404 (NOT_FOUND) status on the /render/generate endpoint means your backend is trying to find a model that simply doesn't exist at that address anymore.
The "v1beta" vs. "v1" Conflict
The error message specifically mentions API version v1beta. While the experimental models lived there, the stable Gemini 3 Flash models usually require the standard v1 endpoint.
To clear this error once and for all, you (or Claude) need to perform these two surgical updates:
Update the Model String
In your render.py (or wherever the model is initialized), replace the experimental string with the stable production version:
Old: models/gemini-2.0-flash-exp
New: models/gemini-3-flash-001 (or simply gemini-3-flash)
Verify the API Endpoint
If you are moving to the direct Gemini API (as we discussed in the "express lane" fix), make sure your backend URL is hitting the stable path:
Endpoint: https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1/models/gemini-3-flash:generateContent?key=YOUR_API_KEY
Why the 502 Bad Gateway?
Notice the 502 (Bad Gateway) error just above the 404. This usually means your frontend (localhost:5173) tried to talk to your Python backend (localhost:8000 or similar), but the Python backend crashed or hung because it couldn't find the model on the Google side.
The chain of events:
Frontend sends render request.
Backend asks Google for gemini-2.0-flash-exp.
Google says "I don't know who that is" (404).
Backend chokes on the 404 and drops the connection.
Frontend sees the dropped connection and reports a 502.
Once you update that model name to Gemini 3, the 502 and 404 should disappear instantly.

The error Unknown name "responseModalities" at 'generation_config' means the API doesn't recognize that field where you've placed it. In the latest Gemini 3 schema, the way you request image output is much stricter.
The Payload Fix
The field responseModalities is often used in the v1beta multimodal chat, but for a direct image generation call in the stable v1 API, the structure needs to be cleaner.
Tell Claude to apply this "Schema Cleanup" to your render.py:
Remove from generation_config: Delete responseModalities from inside the generation_config block. That block is only for settings like temperature or topP.
Use the correct field name: If you are using the multimodal generateContent method to get an image back, the field is usually response_modalities (snake_case) and it sits at the top level of the JSON request, not inside the config.
The Gemini 3 Structure: For the most reliable result, your JSON payload should look like this:
JSON
{ "contents": [ { "parts": [ {"text": "Your simplified archetype prompt here..."}, {"inline_data": {"mime_type": "image/png", "data": "BASE64_MAP_SCREENSHOT"}} ] } ], "generationConfig": { "candidateCount": 1 } }
Why the "Invalid Argument" is happening
The API is essentially saying: "I was ready to work, but you gave me a setting I don't understand, so I have to stop." By removing responseModalities from the config, you stop the validation error. Gemini 3 is smart enough to know that if you are sending a vision request and asking for a render, it should return image data.
A Quick Hack to Test
If you want to bypass the schema headache entirely while Claude is working, you can try setting the model in your backend to just gemini-1.5-flash. It’s more "forgiving" with older payload structures and will help you confirm the connection is solid before you move back up to the high-fidelity Gemini 3.
Once Claude fixes that JSON structure, your POST request should return a 200 OK.

Can you write up a plan of what we need to do next?
Here's the plan for the next phase of render quality improvements:

SiteForge Render Pipeline — Next Steps Plan
1. Building Height Clipping
Problem: Tall buildings in perspective views get clipped at the site boundary polygon edge. The polygon represents the ground-plane footprint, but buildings visually extend above it.
Approach: Instead of canvas-level clip expansion (which we tried and reverted), solve this through prompt engineering — tell Gemini to render buildings as aerial/top-down views that fit within the footprint. Alternatively, explore a smarter clip that extends only the top edge of the boundary upward while keeping sides/bottom tight.
2. Cross-Zone Bleed (Remaining)
Problem: Even with per-zone rendering and prompt instructions, Gemini sometimes extends building content beyond the colored polygon into the white site boundary area, which then overlaps where another zone should be.
Approaches:
Clip building zone renders to a slightly padded version of their polygon (not the full canvas)
Render order refinement — experiment with rendering the site boundary infill (sidewalks, ground-plane) as a first pass, then overlay individual zones
Explore sending a mask alongside the prompt to constrain Gemini's edits more precisely
3. Site Boundary Infill
Problem: The white site boundary area between zones (gaps, margins) doesn't get rendered in per-zone mode since we removed site_boundary from the render queue.
Approach: Add a final "infill pass" that renders only the white gaps with contextual ground-plane (sidewalks, landscaping, small trees) without overwriting the already-rendered zones. This could use a mask that excludes all inner zone polygons.
4. Archetype Shade Colors Not Updating
Problem: When selecting an archetype sub-category (e.g., "Parisian Mid-Rise"), the zone color doesn't update to the unique shade from archetypeShadeMap.ts. Zones keep the default red/green/yellow.
Approach: Fix ZonePropertiesPanel to set zone.color to the archetype's shade when saving. Verify the save mutation passes the color through to the backend.
5. 3D Perspective Consistency
Problem: Renders at steep pitch angles (60°) produce buildings that don't match the surrounding 3D perspective of the Mapbox globe view.
Approach: Include camera pitch/bearing info in the prompt so Gemini matches the viewing angle. For high-pitch views, instruct "oblique aerial view at approximately X degrees."
6. Multi-Pass Compositing Quality
Problem: Per-zone compositing can show visible seams between zones, especially where building shadows should fall onto adjacent park zones.
Approach: Add a final "harmonization pass" — send the fully composited image back to Gemini with a prompt like "Clean up any visible seams, unify lighting and shadows across the entire site."
7. Render Caching & Performance
Problem: Per-zone rendering makes N API calls (one per zone), which is slow for complex sites.
Approaches:
Cache individual zone renders so re-rendering one zone doesn't require re-rendering all
Add a progress indicator showing which zone is currently rendering
Explore batching smaller zones into a single render call
8. Reference Image Support
Problem: The reference image upload exists in the UI but isn't wired into the Gemini prompt.
Approach: Send reference images as additional image parts in the Gemini API call with instructions like "Match the architectural style shown in this reference image."
9. Delete Vertex on Right-Click
Problem: You can add vertices via right-click but can't delete them.
Approach: Right-click on an existing vertex shows a small context menu with "Delete Vertex" option. Minimum 3 vertices enforced.
10. Export & Presentation
Problem: The render result is only available as a PNG download.
Approaches:
Export as georeferenced image (GeoTIFF) for GIS workflows
Side-by-side before/after comparison slider
Export render + zone data as a planning submission package

Priority order: Items 1-4 are the most impactful for render quality. Items 5-6 are polish. Items 7-10 are feature enhancements.
I asked Gemini how we can keep buildings within their specified zones:
To achieve that level of precision—where the AI respects the exact boundaries of your "red zone" while ignoring the purple or green zones—you need to use referential anchoring.
Here is the "perfect" prompt for that specific image:
"Aerial satellite view of the suburban neighborhood from [Image_0]. Keeping the entire map and the purple building area exactly as they are, transform only the area designated by the red polygon into a stone medieval castle. The castle walls and towers must be perfectly contained within the red boundary lines, matching the perspective and 3D footprint of the red volume. Ensure the castle's stone texture and shadows integrate naturally with the surrounding grass and neighboring houses, but do not alter any pixels outside the red zone."
Why this works for spatial accuracy:
Boundary Enforcement: Phrases like "perfectly contained within the red boundary lines" and "3D footprint" tell the model that the red shape isn't just a suggestion—it's a hard limit.
Selective Modification: Explicitly mentioning the "purple building area" and "map" and telling the AI to keep them "exactly as they are" creates a "negative constraint" that protects the rest of your UI.
Contextual Blending: Asking for the "stone texture and shadows" to integrate with the "neighboring houses" ensures the castle looks like it's actually in Calgary, not just photoshopped on top.
UI Awareness: Referring to the "red polygon" or "red volume" acknowledges that you are working with a CAD/planning overlay, which helps the AI understand the geometry.
By using the term "3D footprint," you’re giving the AI a clear geometric constraint that prevents the castle from "bleeding" into the street or the neighboring school field.
A Small "Pro" Refinement:
If you find the AI still struggles to keep the castle inside the lines, you can add one final technical constraint at the end:
"...The castle must be orthographically aligned with the red footprint, ensuring no stone or battlement extends beyond the orange-red base outline."
This forces the model to treat the red area as a containment zone rather than just a general location.

That is the "Perspective Clipping" trap! You’re dealing with the difference between a 2D Footprint (the map) and 3D Parallax (the building leaning over the line).
Because the AI is likely masked to the red lines, it’s "guillotining" the top of your building as soon as the 3D mass crosses the 2D coordinate of the boundary.
To fix this, you have to tell the AI to treat the red boundary as a Ground Floor Footprint, but allow the Vertical Volume to exist in the 3D space above it.
The "Volume-Aware" Prompt
Use this to stop the "guillotine" effect:
"Aerial perspective render based on [Image_0]. Keeping the surrounding neighborhood and purple zone untouched, transform the red area into a [Mediterranean luxury building]. Treat the red boundary as the ground-level footprint only. Allow the building's 3D mass and roofline to extend vertically into the sky, respecting natural perspective even if the upper stories appear to overlap the boundary lines in this 2D view. Do not clip or cut off the building at the site line; render the full 3D structure including the roof and chimneys against the existing background."
Why this solves your specific issue:
"Ground-level footprint only": This tells the AI the red box isn't a "cage" for the whole building, but just the foundation.
"Vertical Volume / Natural Perspective": This gives the AI permission to draw pixels outside the red box if those pixels represent the top of the building leaning toward the camera.
"Do not clip or cut off": This is a direct command to the "safety" or "boundary" logic of the model to prioritize the object's wholeness over the mask's edge.
One Technical Workaround:
If the tool you are using hard-crops the image (meaning it literally won't let pixels generate outside that red line), you may need to manually expand your selection mask by about 20% toward the top of the frame. This "headroom" gives the AI the blank canvas it needs to draw the roof without hitting a "pixel wall."

The Issue: Our system uses a 2D GIS polygon (the red boundary in the provided image) as the hard mask for generative output. Gemini said
To fix the "guillotine" effect where the top of your building is cut off, Claude needs to calculate a Perspective Offset.
In an aerial view, the taller a building is, the further "up" the screen its roof will appear relative to its base. If your mask is strictly tied to the ground coordinates (the red box), the roof is essentially "out of bounds."
Here is the Python logic you can give to Claude Code to help it modify your tool's masking behavior.
The Perspective-Corrected Masking Function
Python
import numpy as np def calculate_perspective_headroom(polygon_coords, building_height_m, camera_pitch_deg): """ Calculates the 'up-screen' expansion needed for a 2D mask to accommodate a 3D building height without clipping. """ # 1. Determine the 'top-most' Y-coordinate of the current red box # In screen space, Y decreases as you move 'up' the image. current_top_y = min(p['y'] for p in polygon_coords) # 2. Calculate the 'Perspective Shift' # As pitch decreases (looking more toward the horizon), # the 'vertical' height takes up more screen Y-space. # height_factor is a simplified ratio of meters to screen pixels pixels_per_meter = 1.5 vertical_shift = (building_height_m * pixels_per_meter) * np.cos(np.radians(camera_pitch_deg)) # 3. Create the 'Headroom' coordinate # We subtract from Y to move the mask boundary 'up' the screen. expanded_top_y = current_top_y - vertical_shift return expanded_top_y # Example usage for Claude: # new_mask_top = calculate_perspective_headroom(red_polygon, 25, 45)
How to use this with the Prompt
When you send this to Claude, tell it to integrate this logic into the Inpainting Mask. Instead of sending just the red polygon to the AI, it should send an "Extended Bounding Box" that looks like this:
Bottom/Sides: Stay locked to the red lines (the "Anchor").
Top: Extends upward by the vertical_shift calculated above.

To help Claude Code implement this, you need to provide a function that translates real-world physics into 2D screen coordinates. Since the camera in your screenshots is at an oblique (angled) aerial perspective, the building's height doesn't just go "up"—it shifts based on the camera's tilt.
Here is the Python logic and the specific prompt for Claude to integrate this into your tool's backend.
The Logic: "Perspective-Shifted Masking"
In an aerial view, a building is a 3D extrusion. While the base stays in the red box, the roof shifts "upward" on the screen. To stop the clipping, the mask must be a "bounding box" that covers both the ground footprint and the projected roof.
Python
import math def get_expanded_mask_for_building(red_polygon_coords, building_height_meters, camera_pitch_deg): """ Calculates the 'headroom' needed to prevent the top of a building from being clipped by a 2D ground-level mask. """ # 1. Identify the 'Highest' point of the red box in screen space (Min Y) min_y = min(p['y'] for p in red_polygon_coords) # 2. Estimate pixels per meter (Calibration constant for your map zoom) # This varies by zoom level, but 2.0 is a good starting 'guess' for this height. ppm = 2.0 # 3. Calculate Vertical Offset (Trigonometry) # The 'flatter' the camera (lower pitch), the more screen space height takes. # Shift = Height * pixels_per_meter * sin(90 - pitch) vertical_offset = building_height_meters * ppm * math.sin(math.radians(90 - camera_pitch_deg)) # 4. Define the New Mask Top # We subtract the offset because Y=0 is the top of the image. expanded_mask_top = min_y - vertical_offset return expanded_mask_top
The Claude Code Implementation Prompt
Copy this into Claude Code to tell it exactly how to update your rendering pipeline:
"I'm sending you a Python function for Perspective-Shifted Masking. Currently, our tool clips 3D buildings because the mask is restricted to the 2D red footprint.
Please update our image generation pipeline with the following logic:
Calculate a 'Headroom Mask': Use the provided function to extend the top edge of the generation mask 'up-screen' based on the building height.
Prompt Injection: Update the system prompt to explicitly tell the AI: 'The red polygon represents the building's foundation. Use the expanded transparent area above the red polygon to render the full 3D vertical mass, rooflines, and architectural details of the building.'
Gaussian Seaming: Apply a 15-pixel feathered edge to the top of the expanded mask. This ensures the new building's roof blends perfectly with the existing 'River Park' background pixels without creating a hard line."
Why this works:
Mathematical Accuracy: It stops "guessing" where the roof is and uses the camera's actual pitch to create space.
Separation of Concerns: It tells the AI the red box is for the foundation but the mask is for the pixels.
Visual Fidelity: The feathered edge (Gaussian blur) prevents that "pasted-on" look at the top of the building.

Here are the key findings for optimizing our Gemini prompts:
Key Takeaways
1. Narrative Prose > Keyword Lists
Google reports 94% scene coherence with narratives vs 61% with keyword lists. Our current prompts are partially keyword-based. We should restructure them as flowing descriptions.
2. Set Temperature to 0
For editing tasks, low temperature = more consistency and better preservation of unedited areas. We're currently not setting temperature.
3. Semantic Masking > Pixel Masks
Gemini can identify what to edit from text alone. Instead of sending a binary mask, we can describe where to edit: "modify only the red colored area." This could simplify our pipeline.
4. Prompt Formula
Subject + Action + Environment + Style + Lighting + Details
Instead of:
"Replace the colored overlay area with a photorealistic parisian mid-rise building..."
Use:
"Aerial photograph of a completed Parisian mid-rise building with cut limestone facade, arched ground-floor retail, wrought iron balconies, and a mansard zinc roof. The building sits naturally within the site, surrounded by sidewalks and mature street trees. Warm afternoon sunlight from the southwest casts crisp shadows. Captured with a DJI drone at 60m altitude, matching the existing satellite imagery perspective."
5. "Keep everything else exactly the same"
Google explicitly recommends this phrase for editing. We're already using it — good.
6. Use Semantic Negatives
Instead of "do NOT add buildings" → say "an empty park with only trees and grass" (positive framing).
7. Output Size
We can request "2K" or even "4K" resolution for higher quality renders.

Perspective Headroom Calculator (calculatePerspectiveHeadroom, line ~574):
function calculatePerspectiveHeadroom(map: MapboxMap, buildingHeightM: number): number {
  const pitch = map.getPitch();
  // Estimate pixels-per-meter at current zoom via map projection
  const p1 = map.project(center);
  const p2 = map.project({ lng: center.lng, lat: center.lat + latOffset });
  const pixelsPerMeter = Math.abs(p2.y - p1.y) / 100;
  const verticalShift = buildingHeightM * pixelsPerMeter * 
    Math.sin(((90 - pitch) * Math.PI) / 180);
  return verticalShift * dpr;
}

  // Draw original polygon + headroom rectangle above it
  ctx.moveTo(minX, expandedTop); ctx.lineTo(maxX, expandedTop);
  ctx.lineTo(maxX, minY); ctx.lineTo(minX, minY);
} else {
  // Ground zones: strict polygon clip
}

For the variants, instead of different weather, it would be good to have slight variations to the different types of buildings e.g. slightly different styles of facades, but for the same general type of building, like having 4 different design types for a high rise glass office tower + the corresponding metadata to match. That makes total sense — instead of 4 weather variants of the same building, you'd have 4 distinct design variations within the same archetype category. Like:
Glass Tower Modern (category) →
Blue Curtain Wall Tower — reflective blue glass, aluminum mullions, rectangular floor plate
All-Glass Faceted Tower — clear low-iron glass, twisted/angular form, expressed white floor slabs
Glass & Steel Diagrid Tower — diamond grid structural steel over glass, tapered form
Glass & Stone Podium Tower — glass upper with limestone-clad podium base, setback terraces
Each with its own unique renderPrompt, facadeDetail, roofDetail, shadeId, and propertyPresets (height, setback, FAR). So when Gemini renders it, the prompt matches exactly which card was selected.
This is actually much more useful than weather variants because:
Students get real design choice within each building type
The render prompts are precisely tailored to each variation
Each variation gets a unique shade color so Gemini can distinguish them on the map
The propertyPresets can vary too (e.g., a diagrid tower might be taller than a rectangular one)
So instead of 77 archetypes × 4 weather shots, we're talking 77 archetypes × 4 design variations = ~308 total archetype cards, each with unique metadata.

Absolutely — the card images are just for the UI picker. What really matters is the render prompt metadata that gets sent to Gemini when someone hits render. Each variant's renderPrompt.mapOverlay needs to be optimized for:
Aerial/drone perspective (not eye-level like the cards) — because the actual render replaces a colored polygon on a satellite/drone photo
Polygon-aware language — "Replace the [color] polygon with..." and "The [color] area is the building's ground-level foundation..."
Scale and containment — explicit height, floor count, footprint behavior, "do not extend beyond the polygon horizontally"
Roof/aerial appearance — since drone view primarily sees rooftops, materials, shadows, parking, landscaping from above
Materials that read from above — roof color, facade visible at oblique angles, ground-plane treatment around the building
The card images use eye-level prompts for visual appeal in the picker. The renderPrompt uses aerial prompts for actual rendering. Two completely separate prompt systems.

Neither — these card images are purely for the UI picker (so users can visually browse and select an archetype). The actual site render uses a completely different pipeline and prompt system.

Eye-level, 3/4 angle, watercolor illustration style

Aerial/oblique drone perspective looking down

Even better, Mapbox can natively generate the perfect clipping mask for you by manipulating layer visibility before taking the screenshot.

The Paradigm Shift: The "Isolate & Snapshot" Workflow
Instead of doing math, Claude will script Mapbox to take two screenshots sequentially:
The Base Render (The Proxy Block): Mapbox extrudes your red polygon into a solid light-grey 3D block. It takes a screenshot of the map with this block sitting on it. This gives the AI the perfect perspective, lighting, and volume reference.
The Perfect Mask (The Silhouette): Claude temporarily hides the satellite map, turns the map background pure black, and turns the 3D building pure white. It takes a second screenshot. This is your flawless, pixel-perfect 3D mask. No math required.

Context: We are using Mapbox GL JS to feed a generative AI (Nano Banana 2) for architectural inpainting. We need to eliminate 3D roof clipping by using Mapbox's native fill-extrusion to create a spatial proxy, rather than relying on 2D polygon footprint math.
Task for Claude Code: Implement an asynchronous "Isolate & Snapshot" pipeline in our Mapbox viewer before sending the API call to the image generator.
Step 1: Create the 3D Proxy (Base Image)

Here is the exact Mapbox GL JS implementation logic you can hand over to Claude.
To make this work seamlessly, Claude needs to wrap Mapbox's event listeners in async/await Promises. This ensures the code waits for the 3D map to finish drawing before taking the screenshots.
Copy and paste this technical brief directly to Claude Code:
TASK: IMPLEMENT MAPBOX GL JS "ISOLATE & SNAPSHOT" WORKFLOW
Objective: > Create a JavaScript module that uses our Mapbox instance to generate two base64 images (A Base 3D Render and a perfect Alpha Mask) to send to our generative AI pipeline.
Critical Requirement: > Ensure the Mapbox instance was initialized with preserveDrawingBuffer: true, otherwise map.getCanvas().toDataURL() will return a blank image.
Please implement the following Async Workflow:
Helper Function: Wait for Render
Create a Promise-based helper to pause execution until Mapbox finishes drawing.
JavaScript
const waitForMapIdle = (map) => new Promise(resolve => map.once('idle', resolve));
Step 1: Draw the Proxy & Take Base Snapshot
Inject the 3D polygon, wait for the render, and capture the context.
JavaScript
// 1. Add the polygon source (assuming 'buildingGeoJSON' is the user's selected footprint) map.addSource('ai-proxy-source', { type: 'geojson', data: buildingGeoJSON }); // 2. Add the 3D extrusion layer map.addLayer({ 'id': 'ai-proxy-building', 'type': 'fill-extrusion', 'source': 'ai-proxy-source', 'paint': { 'fill-extrusion-color': '#dddddd', // Neutral matte grey 'fill-extrusion-height': ['get', 'height'], // e.g., 20 meters 'fill-extrusion-opacity': 1.0 } }); // 3. Wait for Mapbox to draw the 3D block await waitForMapIdle(map); // 4. Capture the Base Image const baseImageBase64 = map.getCanvas().toDataURL('image/png');
Step 2: Generate the Silhouette Mask
Iterate through all layers to hide the background, turn the background black, and turn our proxy building pure white.
JavaScript
// 1. Store original states so we can revert later const originalStates = {}; // 2. Hide all layers except our proxy map.getStyle().layers.forEach(layer => { if (layer.id !== 'ai-proxy-building' && layer.id !== 'temporary-black-bg') { originalStates[layer.id] = map.getLayoutProperty(layer.id, 'visibility') || 'visible'; map.setLayoutProperty(layer.id, 'visibility', 'none'); } }); // 3. Add a pure black background layer at the very bottom map.addLayer({ 'id': 'temporary-black-bg', 'type': 'background', 'paint': { 'background-color': '#000000' } }, 'ai-proxy-building'); // insert beneath the proxy // 4. Turn the proxy building pure white map.setPaintProperty('ai-proxy-building', 'fill-extrusion-color', '#ffffff'); // 5. Wait for the style changes to render await waitForMapIdle(map); // 6. Capture the Mask Image const maskImageBase64 = map.getCanvas().toDataURL('image/png');
Step 3: Cleanup
Revert the map back to its original state for the user.
JavaScript
// 1. Remove the black background map.removeLayer('temporary-black-bg'); // 2. Restore all original layer visibilities Object.keys(originalStates).forEach(layerId => { if (map.getLayer(layerId)) { map.setLayoutProperty(layerId, 'visibility', originalStates[layerId]); } }); // 3. (Optional) Remove the proxy building if you want the map clean, // or leave it if you want to swap it with the AI result later. map.removeLayer('ai-proxy-building'); map.removeSource('ai-proxy-source');
Final Output: Package baseImageBase64 and maskImageBase64 into the payload sent to the Image Generation API endpoint.
Why this specific code is bulletproof:
The waitForMapIdle Promise: This is the most common pitfall when exporting from Mapbox. If you don't wait for the idle event, you end up capturing half-rendered map tiles.
The Temporary Black Background: Mapbox canvases are often transparent by default. If you just hide the satellite imagery, the mask might export with a transparent background instead of black, which confuses the AI. Injecting a hard black background layer guarantees a perfect, high-contrast silhouette.
By giving Claude this exact logic, it won't waste time trying to figure out Mapbox's WebGL canvas quirks. It can just wire this directly into your UI button!

const MIN_RENDER_WIDTH = 2048;
async function captureMapCanvasBase64(map: MapboxMap): Promise<string> {
  const canvas = map.getCanvas();
  const w = canvas.width;
  const h = canvas.height;
  const scale = w < MIN_RENDER_WIDTH ? MIN_RENDER_WIDTH / w : 1;
  const targetW = Math.round(w * scale);
  const targetH = Math.round(h * scale);
  // ... upscale via offscreen canvas if scale > 1
}

Also - Here is info from Gemini on how to make the aesthetic styles better. See below. Please implement.
Here is a breakdown of the architectural aesthetics shown in your interface, along with detailed prompts designed to generate these specific styles using an AI image generator.
To keep the examples consistent, I've used a base subject of a "modern mid-rise mixed-use building with a public plaza" for all the prompts. You can easily swap out this core subject for a streetscape, a park, or a specific massing concept.
Photo Realistic
Aesthetic: Emulates high-end architectural photography. It focuses on physical accuracy, lifelike materials (glass reflections, concrete texture), realistic global illumination, and high-quality entourage (people, cars, trees).
Gemini Prompt: > A hyper-realistic exterior architectural rendering of a modern mid-rise mixed-use building with an active public plaza. Cinematic lighting, golden hour sunlight casting realistic shadows. Highly detailed materials including reflective glass facades and textured concrete. Lush, realistic landscaping and a lively street scene with diverse pedestrians. 8k resolution, ray-traced lighting, professional architectural photography.
Drone Photo
Aesthetic: Captures the project from an elevated, aerial vantage point. It emphasizes the building's relationship to its surrounding urban context, roof plans, and overall footprint.
Gemini Prompt: > An aerial drone photograph of a modern mid-rise mixed-use building. Shot from 200 feet in the air, angled downwards at a 45-degree angle. The image shows the building situated within a realistic urban context with surrounding streets, neighboring rooftops, and traffic. Sunny day, clear cast shadows, high-resolution aerial photography.
Massing Study
Aesthetic: A conceptual stage representation focusing purely on volume, form, scale, and spatial relationships, usually stripping away material details and colors. Often rendered in plain white or "clay."
Gemini Prompt: > An architectural massing study of a mid-rise mixed-use development. Rendered entirely as plain, untextured matte white blocks on a neutral grey background. No windows or material details. Focus strictly on volume, form, and scale. Clean ambient occlusion lighting with sharp directional sunlight to show deep shadows. Minimalist architectural diagram style.
Site Plan
Aesthetic: A 2D orthographic, top-down view used to show the layout of a parcel of land. It illustrates building footprints, pathways, landscaping, and boundaries, often using flat colors and stylized symbols.
Gemini Prompt: > A top-down 2D architectural site plan of a mixed-use building and surrounding public plaza. Strict orthographic projection, looking straight down. Clean architectural linework, soft flat pastel colors. Stylized trees depicted as simple green overlapping circles. Paved pathways, defined property lines, and crisp shadows indicating building height. Professional urban planning drawing.
Ink Wash
Aesthetic: A traditional artistic medium utilizing diluted ink applied with a brush. It creates atmospheric, moody, and expressive images with fluid gradients, usually in monochromatic black, grey, or sepia tones.
Gemini Prompt: > An expressive architectural ink wash painting of a modern mid-rise building. Monochromatic black and grey tones on heavy textured watercolor paper. Diluted ink gradients, atmospheric perspective, loose and fluid brushstrokes. A moody, artistic, and conceptual architectural illustration.
Charcoal
Aesthetic: A rough, high-contrast, and dramatic sketch style. It features smudged shadows, heavy black lines, and the distinct texture of the paper showing through the strokes. Excellent for emphasizing light and dark values.
Gemini Prompt: > A dramatic charcoal sketch of a modern mid-rise building. Rendered on rough textured paper with deep black smudged shadows and expressive, gestural line work. High contrast black and white. Focus on the interplay of stark light and heavy shadow, artistic and raw architectural drawing style.
Marker Render
Aesthetic: Emulates the classic hand-drawn presentation style using tools like Copic markers and fine-liner pens. It features crisp ink outlines overlaid with vibrant, transparent strokes of layered color.
Gemini Prompt: > A traditional architectural marker rendering of a modern mixed-use building. Classic Copic marker style with crisp fine-liner black ink outlines. Layered, transparent color strokes with visible marker overlap. Bright, optimistic lighting, stylized architectural entourage and trees. Professional design presentation sketch aesthetic.
Isometric
Aesthetic: A 3D representation where all parallel lines remain parallel (no perspective distortion). It provides a clean, easily readable diagrammatic view of spaces, often used in UI, exploded views, or spatial diagrams.
Gemini Prompt: > An isometric 3D architectural diagram of a modern mixed-use building and plaza. Clean parallel projection with zero perspective distortion. Rendered in smooth matte pastel colors. Clear spatial layout, vector-art aesthetic, highly detailed, precise, and visually pleasing architectural graphic.
Wood Block
Aesthetic: Inspired by traditional printmaking. It features bold, chunky black outlines, flat areas of limited color, and a distinct, rough wood grain texture overlaying the image. Very graphic and stylized.
Gemini Prompt: > A stylized woodblock print of an urban mid-rise building. Bold, thick black outlines, a flat and limited vintage color palette. Visible wood grain texture heavily integrated into the image. Graphic, retro, and stylized architectural illustration with a strong, balanced composition.
Water Colour
Aesthetic: Soft, airy, and artistic. It is characterized by translucent washes of color, bleeding edges where colors mix, and a slightly unpredictable, organic feel. Great for selling the "mood" of a space.
Gemini Prompt: > A beautiful watercolor architectural painting of a modern mixed-use building and plaza. Soft bleeding edges, translucent layered color washes. Bright, airy, and inviting atmosphere. Loose and artistic representation, painted on highly textured watercolor paper.
Would you like to test a few of these prompts right now to see how the outputs look, or perhaps adjust the base subject to something specific you are working on?
Show more

Idea I want to get your thoughts on - don't code, I just want to see if you think this is a good idea / feasible:
My conversation with Gemini:
It would be great to see street views of the development. It would be similar to dropping pegman to see street view, but it just generates one street view render
Gemini said
That is an excellent feature idea. Bridging the gap between top-down, bird's-eye master plans and the actual human-scale experience of a street is one of the biggest challenges in urban design. Giving users a familiar, intuitive interaction—like dropping a pin or a "Pegman"—to instantly visualize the streetscape would be incredibly powerful for stakeholders and designers alike.
Here is a breakdown of how you could conceptualize and build this feature:
The UX/UI Flow
The "Drop" Interaction: The user selects a distinct icon (a pedestrian figure, a camera, or a pin) from the toolbar and drags it onto the 2D plan.
Snapping Constraints: To ensure the generated view makes sense, the tool should ideally snap the icon to defined public right-of-ways, sidewalks, or plazas, rather than the middle of a building mass.
Directional Control: Once dropped, the user needs to establish a line of sight. This could be a conical field-of-view indicator that the user can rotate 360 degrees to choose what the camera is looking at.
The Output Modal: After setting the angle, a modal or side-panel slides in, displaying the rendered street view.
Technical Implementation Approaches
Generating the actual visual output will depend on how your application handles data.
The Generative AI Approach (Fast & Conceptual) Instead of relying on heavy, textured 3D models, you can use the map's 2D data to guide an AI image generator.
How it works: When the pin is dropped, the system calculates the camera's view. It extracts a basic wireframe or depth map of the building masses in that field of view.
The Magic: You pass this structural outline into an API (like ControlNet/Stable Diffusion) along with a text prompt generated from the plan's metadata (e.g., "Street level view, 5-story residential building, brick facade, street trees, sunny day, pedestrian-friendly").
Pros: Produces highly evocative, photorealistic conceptual renders in seconds without needing fully modeled architecture.
The WebGL / 3D Engine Approach (Accurate & Volumetric) If your tool is already generating 3D massings, you can position a virtual camera at the exact coordinates.
How it works: The system drops a camera object into the three-dimensional scene at a height of about 1.7 meters (human eye level).
The Output: It captures a snapshot of the raw 3D geometry (the extruded blocks).
Pros: 100% spatially accurate to the master plan. You can enhance it by applying simple procedural textures (e.g., standard glass textures for commercial ground floors, solid colors for residential).
Expanding the Value
To make this feature even more useful for urban planning, you could include a data overlay on the generated image. While the user looks at the rendering, a small sidebar could display the metrics for that specific street segment: road width, setback distances, and zoning density.
Would you like to brainstorm the UI layout for how the user interacts with this tool, or would you prefer to dive into the logic of translating map coordinates into a generated scene?
You said
Yes - using the data from the image cards and the spatial data from the polygons and polylines.
Gemini said
This is a brilliant way to leverage the data you are already organizing in the software. By combining the precise geometry of the polylines and polygons with the stylistic intent of the image cards, you can generate a highly accurate and evocative street-level render.
Here is a logical pipeline for how you can translate that 2D map data into a synthesized 3D street view.
The Geometry Engine (Raycasting the View Cone)
When the user drops the "Pegman" pin and sets an angle, the system needs to determine what is actually visible from that specific vantage point.
Establish the Camera: Record the pin's X,Y coordinates and the directional angle. Assume a standard human eye-level height (e.g., 1.7 meters).
Cast the View Cone: Project a 2D triangle or cone from the pin outwards, representing the camera's field of view (typically around 60 to 90 degrees).
Calculate Intersections: Run a spatial query to find all polylines (roads, paths) and polygons (building footprints, parks, plazas) that intersect with this view cone.
Determine Depth and Scale: Calculate the distance from the pin to each intersecting object to establish foreground, midground, and background elements.
The Semantic Translation (Applying the Image Cards)
Once the system knows what geometry is in the frame, it needs to know what that geometry looks like. This is where your image cards come in.
Fetch Metadata: For every polygon and polyline in the view cone, retrieve its associated data.
Extract Typology: Pull the specific attributes defined by the user's assigned image cards. For a polygon, this might be "6-story mixed-use," "brick facade," or "retail ground floor." For a polyline, it might be "protected bike lane," "street trees," or "cobblestone."
Height Extrusion: Check the height or floor-count attribute of the polygons so the system knows how tall to scale the buildings in the generated view.
Creating the Structural Guide (The Control Map)
AI image generators need more than just text to maintain spatial accuracy; they need a structural foundation so buildings don't appear in the middle of the street.
Generate a Depth Map or Segmentation Map: Use the intersecting geometry and height data to draw a very rudimentary, untextured 3D block model from the camera's perspective.
Color-Code the Map: If using semantic segmentation (like ControlNet), color the ground plane gray, the extruded building polygons red, and the sky blue.
Purpose: This rough image acts as a rigid scaffold. You feed it to the AI to say, "Put the buildings exactly here, and put the street exactly here."
Dynamic Prompt Generation
Simultaneously, the system compiles a text prompt to feed to the image generator, using the data extracted from the image cards.
Base Formula: The system concatenates the data into a cohesive string.
Example Output: Eye-level street view, [Polyline data: 2-lane road with wide sidewalks and street trees], flanked by [Polygon 1 data: 4-story residential townhomes with modern wood siding], and [Polygon 2 data: neighborhood park], sunny, photorealistic, architectural rendering.
The API Execution
Finally, the tool sends the dynamically generated text prompt and the structural Control Map to an image generation API. The AI uses the prompt for style and materials, and the Control Map for precise spatial boundaries, returning a street view that accurately reflects the master plan's data.

Plaintext
Act as a senior full-stack spatial software engineer. I am building a master planning software tool. I need you to write the logic and component structure for a new feature called "Street View Render." ### Feature Overview The user drags and drops a "Pegman" icon onto a 2D canvas (the site boundary area). Once dropped, the user rotates the Pegman to set a viewing angle. The system then calculates a "view cone," identifies which spatial elements (polygons representing building masses/parks, and polylines representing roads/paths) fall within that cone, extracts their associated metadata ("image cards"), and packages this into a payload to be sent to an AI image generation API. Please provide the code and architecture for the following three core requirements: ### Requirement 1: The Raycasting & View Cone Math Write the utility functions to calculate what geometry falls within the user's field of view. Assume a 2D Cartesian coordinate system. * Camera Position: $(x_c, y_c)$ based on the dropped Pegman. * Viewing Direction: An angle $\theta$ (in radians) representing where the Pegman is facing. * Field of View (FOV): A constant angle $\phi$ (e.g., $\frac{\pi}{3}$ for 60 degrees). * View Distance: A maximum rendering distance $d_{max}$. The logic must: 1. Calculate the left and right boundary vectors of the view cone: $\theta - \frac{\phi}{2}$ and $\theta + \frac{\phi}{2}$. 2. Iterate through the canvas elements (arrays of polylines and polygons). 3. Return an array of elements that intersect with or are contained within this cone, sorted by distance from $(x_c, y_c)$ to determine foreground vs. background. ### Requirement 2: The Data Extraction & JSON Structure Once the visible geometry is identified, write the function that maps the master plan's data into a structured JSON payload. The application uses "Image Cards"—metadata objects attached to the polygons and polylines. Generate the TypeScript interfaces and the transformation logic to output a payload that looks exactly like this: { "scene_config": { "camera_coords": { "x": 105.2, "y": 402.8 }, "facing_angle": 45, "fov": 60 }, "visible_environment": [ { "element_id": "poly_847", "distance_from_camera": 12.5, "geometry_type": "polygon", "image_card_data": { "typology": "mixed-use", "height_floors": 5, "facade_material": "red brick", "ground_level": "retail storefronts with awnings" } }, { "element_id": "line_22", "distance_from_camera": 2.0, "geometry_type": "polyline", "image_card_data": { "typology": "street", "width_meters": 10, "features": ["protected bike lane", "street trees"] } } ] } ### Requirement 3: The Prompt Construction Generator Write a function that parses the JSON payload generated in Requirement 2 and dynamically constructs a natural language prompt string. The function should: 1. Set a base photographic style (e.g., "Photorealistic eye-level architectural street view render, sunny day, highly detailed..."). 2. Concatenate the data from the visible_environment array, prioritizing items with the lowest distance_from_camera to describe the immediate foreground first. 3. Translate the height_floors into descriptive massing (e.g., "A 5-story mixed-use building"). 4. Output the final string ready for an API like Stable Diffusion or Midjourney. Please provide modular, well-commented code for these three steps, separating the spatial math from the data transformation.
This prompt gives Claude the exact mathematical boundaries it needs for the spatial queries, while also tightly defining the data structure so it plugs perfectly into your existing polygon/polyline framework.

Research complete. Here's what I found — there are 4 critical root causes for why parks don't show up well:
Root Cause Analysis
1. Parks & Streets Have ZERO Metadata (Critical)
The street view hook only imports buildingArchetypes.json. It never imports openSpaceArchetypes.json or streetPathArchetypes.json. So when it looks up a park archetype like urban_pocket_park, the lookup fails silently and returns {} — no landscape character, no planting description, no surface type. Buildings get 5+ sentences of rich facade/material detail while parks get nothing.
2. Parks Drawn Too Small in Depth Map
In the guide image, parks are rendered as thin ground-plane trapezoids regardless of distance. A park 15m away looks the same height as one 100m away. Buildings get tall rectangles; parks get compressed slivers near the horizon.
3. No Tree Canopy Representation
Parks have no vertical element in the depth map. In reality, a park 20m away would show large tree canopies filling much of the frame. The depth map shows flat green strips.
4. Prompt Doesn't Emphasize Parks
Since park metadata is empty, the prompt says something like "Green Space / Park" while a building next to it gets "5-story building with warm light brick, recessed glass storefront, stone cornice..." — Gemini naturally prioritizes the detailed description.

Great research document. Here are my key takeaways relevant to our street view feature, and what I'd caveat:
What's Useful
1. Narrative prompts beat keyword dumps for Flash 2.5 — This validates our approach of writing flowing scene descriptions rather than comma-separated tags. But we should restructure our prompt to read more like a cinematic scene description with relational prepositions ("adjacent to," "receding into the background") rather than the structured data format we're currently using.
2. Z-axis depth partitioning — The foreground/midground/background separation we're already doing is the right approach. But the PDF suggests using cinematic language: "In the foreground, [description]. In the midground, [description]. In the background, [description]." — a flowing narrative, not labeled sections.
3. Camera/lens directives — Specifying "35mm lens, f/8, eye-level" triggers specific perspective geometry in the model. We're doing some of this but could be more precise.
4. Affirmative framing — The model handles "describe what IS there" far better than "don't do X." Our prohibitions list is working against us — we should minimize negatives.
5. The depth map as reference image — The PDF confirms multi-image fusion works well when you explicitly define relationships ("Take the spatial layout from image 1 and apply the materials described in the text").
What I'd Caveat
"Nano Banana Pro" / "Gemini 3 Pro Image" — I can't verify these model names exist in the actual Gemini API. The document references them confidently but Gemini has a pattern of hallucinating model names and architectures. We should stick with gemini-2.5-flash-image which is confirmed working.
The SCHEMA methodology — The arXiv paper reference (2602.18903) may be real, but the 91%/94% compliance stats and "850 verified predictions" should be taken with a grain of salt from a Gemini-generated research document.
Recommended Further Research

Here is an in-depth breakdown of how to achieve maximum spatial accuracy and architectural precision using the gemini-3-pro-image-preview API.
Unlike the 2.5 Flash model which relies on narrative intuition, Gemini 3 Pro Image (commercially known as Nano Banana Pro) operates as a highly deterministic, reasoning-driven engine.
Reference Image Conditioning
While the Flash model benefits greatly from semantic segmentation masks, Gemini 3 Pro Image features advanced reasoning that allows it to process raw architectural inputs with remarkable fidelity.
Optimal Formats: The model excels when provided with orthographic blueprints, flat-lay CAD plans, or wireframe sketches. It can interpret these structural guidelines and generate mathematically accurate architectural views (Plan, Elevation, and Section).
Multi-Image Fusion: The Pro model's standout capability is its massive input capacity, supporting up to 14 reference images simultaneously in a single prompt. You can upload a simple structural wireframe alongside separate images of specific textures (e.g., a specific wood grain or marble) and command the model to map the uploaded textures strictly to the geometry of the wireframe.
Prompt Structure for Multi-Object Scenes
If you use flowing narrative descriptions with the Pro model, you are underutilizing its architecture. The gemini-3-pro-image-preview model responds best to command-line style syntax and structured JSON.
Command-Line Syntax: To maximize spatial control, prompts should strip away polite, conversational filler and use rigid constraint lists (e.g., explicitly listing "Mandatory" elements and "Prohibitions").
JSON & Grid Layouts: For multi-object placement, the model respects mathematical grid commands. By defining a canvas as a "3x3 grid layout" and assigning contents to specific cells, you can perfectly isolate elements. Furthermore, developers can pass strict JSON schemas to force the model to output specific elements or annotations exactly where instructed without hallucinating extra details.
Perspective and Depth Control
Gemini 3 Pro achieves what the technical documentation calls "Coordinate-Level Accuracy".
Optical Simulation: Rather than using vague terms like "far away," distance scaling and one-point perspective are enforced by simulating physical camera optics. You should explicitly define the lens focal length, aperture, and shutter speed in the prompt to create realistic volumetric depth (e.g., "50mm lens, f/8 aperture, deep focus").
Relative Positioning: The reasoning engine understands explicit geometric and relative positioning commands, allowing you to anchor objects with mathematical precision relative to the boundaries of the canvas.
Real-World Case Studies
Several production environments heavily utilize gemini-3-pro-image-preview specifically for its structural control:
Finnish-it (Language App): This application uses the Pro model for an automated image annotation pipeline. By passing a strict JSON schema, the app forces the model to generate a complex scene (like an urban street) and apply perfectly positioned text labels and pointing lines to specific objects. The model actively calculates negative space to ensure no annotation lines cross each other, a feat of spatial reasoning.
Designforge-ai: This platform utilizes the Pro model as an "Image Studio" agent to generate high-fidelity, dimensionally accurate UI placeholders, architectural assets, and website hero sections based on technical specifications.
Paper2Slides: An open-source academic tool that uses the Pro model to render complex "blueprint" style diagrams and 3D process pipelines, utilizing the model's ability to logically organize scientific spatial layouts.
API Parameters & The "Thinking" Engine
The API configuration for the Pro model differs significantly from the 2.5 Flash pipeline:
thinking_level: Unlike Gemini 2.5 which used a numerical thinking_budget (that could be disabled), Gemini 3 models utilize the thinking_level parameter, which accepts string values like LOW, MEDIUM, or HIGH. For complex architectural rendering and multi-object spatial math, this should be set to HIGH. Note that thinking cannot be turned off for the gemini-3-pro-image-preview model.
media_resolution: A new parameter introduced in the Gemini 3 API. For generating or analyzing dense architectural plans, setting this to media_resolution_high forces the model to allocate up to 1120 tokens per image, ensuring maximum spatial detail extraction.
seed: Fixing the random seed is explicitly required for professional workflows. Once a baseline architectural layout is achieved, locking the seed allows you to reliably swap materials or change the time of day without altering the underlying spatial geometry.

Tell me more about item #1
Clay Render Generator — The Concept
Right now, our street view depth map looks like this: flat colored rectangles drawn on a 2D canvas from a top-down perspective, then sent to Gemini as a reference image. Gemini has to guess what the 3D perspective should look like — building heights, occlusion (which building is in front of which), and scale.
A clay render would instead generate a proper 3D perspective view from the pegman's eye level. Think of it like a simple 3D video game scene with gray boxes:
What we send now:          What a clay render would send:
┌──────────────┐           
│  ┌──┐  ┌───┐│                ┌─────────┐
│  │red│  │grn││           ┌──┐│         │
│  └──┘  └───┘│           │  ││  gray   │
│     ┌────┐  │           │  ││  box    │
│     │blue│  │           │  │└─────────┘
│     └────┘  │           └──┘
└──────────────┘           ▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀▀
  (flat 2D map)            (3D perspective from eye level)
How it would work:
Take the pegman's position and facing direction
For each zone in the view cone, we already know:
The polygon coordinates (lat/lng → converted to meters relative to pegman)
The zone type (building = extruded box, park = flat green plane, water = flat blue plane)
Building height (from minFloors/maxFloors × ~3.5m per floor)
Project those 3D volumes onto a 2D canvas using simple perspective math — camera at 1.7m height, looking in the facing direction
Render each volume as a solid gray box with slight shading (lighter on sun-facing side, darker on shadow side) — no textures, no colors, just geometry
Send this gray perspective image as Image 0 to Gemini
Why this is a game-changer:
Gemini no longer guesses heights — a 20-story tower renders as a tall gray box, a 2-story house as a small one
Occlusion is explicit — if a park is behind a building, the building's gray box physically covers it. Gemini can't put the park in front
Scale is locked — nearby buildings are large in the frame, distant ones are small. No more "the lanehouse 200m away looks as big as the garden 10m away"
No sketch bias — the research found that line drawings trigger Gemini's illustration aesthetic. Solid gray volumes suppress that and let the text prompt control the style
Implementation options (lightest to heaviest):
2D Canvas with manual perspective math (~50 lines of code) — project 3D coordinates to 2D using a simple pinhole camera model. Fast, no dependencies, but no proper hidden surface removal
Three.js offscreen render (~100 lines) — create a Three.js scene with BoxGeometry for each building, PlaneGeometry for parks/water, position a PerspectiveCamera at eye level, render to an offscreen canvas. Proper z-buffering, lighting, occlusion — all handled automatically
Use the existing Mapbox GL 3D extrusions — your map already shows 3D extruded buildings. Could potentially capture that view, but the camera would need to be repositioned to street level which Mapbox doesn't do well
My recommendation: Three.js offscreen render. You already have Three.js in the project (it's used in SiteZonesGroup.tsx), so no new dependencies. It handles all the hard parts (z-buffering, perspective projection, lighting) and would render in <50ms. The output would be a clean gray massing model from the exact pegman viewpoint.

Lower Impact / Future:

I think some aesthetic styles render better than others. Why would that be?
A few reasons:
The prompt structure favors photorealistic styles — Our prompts say "DJI drone at 60m altitude" and "aerial photograph" which strongly anchors Gemini toward photorealism. When you select Watercolour or Wood Block, the style modifier has to fight against that photorealistic framing. The artistic styles that work best (like Wood Block) have strong enough visual identity to override it, while weaker ones get pulled back toward photo-realism.
Pass 1 vs Pass 2 style consistency — The ground plane renders in the selected style, but then Pass 2 buildings render on top of that result. If Pass 1 produces a watercolour ground, Pass 2 might render a photorealistic building on top because it's using the rendered ground as its base image — and Gemini tries to match the "photo" it sees.
The archetype card photos are photorealistic — We're sending archetype card thumbnails (real architectural photos) as reference images. When Gemini sees a photo of a glass office tower, it wants to render it photorealistically regardless of the style modifier. For artistic styles, we should probably skip sending the archetype cards or send stylized versions instead.
Style modifier strength varies — Some of our GEMINI_STYLE_MODIFIERS are short/vague while others are detailed. The more specific the style description, the better Gemini follows it.
Quick fixes I could make:
Skip archetype card images when using artistic styles (so Gemini isn't pulled toward photorealism)
Put the style instruction FIRST in the prompt instead of last (Gemini weighs earlier instructions more heavily)
Strengthen the weaker style modifiers
Want me to try any of these?

Great idea. Based on the metadata we have (facade materials, roof descriptions, color schemes, landscape character, planting types) and what works well at street-level perspective, here are my top recommendations:
Best 3 for Street View:
Watercolour — Your archetype metadata is rich in material descriptions (sandstone, timber, glass, raked gravel). Watercolour renders beautifully at street level because the soft washes highlight material textures and the loose edges make landscape elements (trees, water) feel natural. The golden hour lighting we use works perfectly with warm watercolour palettes.
Charcoal / Pencil Sketch — Street-level perspectives are where architectural sketches shine — it's how architects actually present designs to clients. Your facade detail metadata (window patterns, balcony railings, ground floor treatments) translates perfectly into line weight variation. The depth we've built into the SCHEMA prompts (foreground sharp, background hazy) maps naturally to charcoal's tonal range.
Marker Render — This is the classic architectural presentation style — bold felt-tip markers with visible strokes. It works exceptionally well at street level because it emphasizes building massing and material contrast (glass vs brick vs wood) which is exactly what your archetype cards describe. The warm/cool color separation in marker renders makes parks and water features pop against buildings.
Why these 3 over others:
Ink Wash and Wood Block are more suited to aerial/bird's eye views
Massing Study and Site Plan are analytical, not presentation-quality
Isometric breaks the street-level perspective entirely
Drone Photo is just photorealistic from a different angle

Excellent research. Here are the key takeaways for SiteForge:
Biggest Insight — Style Position in Prompt Matters:
The research confirms what we just discovered — if style is placed at the beginning, the model weights aesthetics heavily (sometimes at the expense of accuracy). If placed at the end, it prioritizes structural fidelity. Our current approach of putting it FIRST is correct for artistic styles since we want the style to dominate. For photorealistic, we leave it at the end.
Actionable Improvements for Our Styles:
Watercolour — Our prompt is missing key triggers: "wet-on-wet technique", "unpainted paper as highlights" (watercolourists can't paint white), "jittery ink pen linework" for outlines. The research says lighting should use "negative space of unpainted paper" not digital shadows.
Charcoal/Sketch — We should add "edges fade out loosely into white paper" for the unfinished sketchbook aesthetic. Also "architectural crosshatching" is a strong trigger we're missing.
Marker — We need "overlapping streaky marker strokes", "ink bleed at edges", and critically "white gaps left between strokes to represent highlights". Our prompt has most of this but could be stronger.
New Styles Worth Adding:
Oil on Canvas — "thick impasto technique", "palette knife", "chiaroscuro lighting". Great for dramatic presentations.
Clay/White Model — Pure white massing with ambient occlusion only. Perfect for planning authority presentations.
Collage — Post-digital mixed media. Very trendy in architecture competitions.
Technical Insight — Positive Framing:
The research confirms AI models struggle with "don't do X" instructions. Instead of "no photorealistic elements", say "render entirely in watercolour medium." This explains why some of our negative constraints haven't been working well.
Want me to update the 4 style prompts with these insights, or commit what we have first and refine later?

Good question. Here are the specific research gaps that would help me get the last 5%:

Prompt for Gemini Deep Research:
I am building an urban planning tool (SiteForge) that generates street-level architectural renders using the Gemini API. I send a 3D clay massing model (gray boxes representing buildings, green for parks, blue for water) alongside a structured text prompt describing each zone. The renders are 90% there but I need to solve these final consistency issues:
Research Question 1: Preventing hallucinated/random buildings
When I ask Gemini to render a scene with 3-4 specific buildings, it sometimes adds extra buildings that don't exist in my site plan — random towers in the background, buildings between zones, etc. What are the most effective prompt techniques to prevent Gemini from hallucinating additional structures? Are there specific negative prompt phrases, generation config parameters (temperature, top_k, top_p), or reference image techniques that constrain the model to ONLY render what's described? Provide tested approaches with the gemini-2.5-flash-image and gemini-3-pro-image-preview models specifically.
Research Question 2: Spatial consistency between re-renders
When I re-render the same scene (same pegman position, same direction, same zones), the spatial layout changes significantly each time — buildings swap sides, parks move, relative sizes change. Beyond seed locking (which doesn't work for image models), what techniques produce the most consistent spatial output across multiple generations? Does lowering temperature help? Does providing the clay massing model as Image 1 vs Image 2 matter? Does prompt ordering affect spatial consistency? Provide quantitative comparisons if available.
Research Question 3: Accurate left/right/foreground/background placement
I describe zones as "LEFT side of frame (15%-40%)" or "RIGHT side (60%-85%)" but Gemini often swaps left and right, or puts foreground elements in the background. What is the most effective way to communicate precise spatial positioning to Gemini image models? Options I'm considering:
Percentage-based frame positioning (current approach)
Clock-face positioning ("the office building is at the 2 o'clock position")
Relative positioning ("the garden is directly in front, the office is to the right of the garden")
Grid-cell assignment ("place the office in cell B3 of a 3x3 grid")
Color-coded reference image with explicit color-to-zone mapping
Which approach has the highest spatial adherence rate? Provide tested examples.
Research Question 4: Temperature and generation config for architectural scenes
What are the optimal temperature, top_k, and top_p values for architectural rendering specifically? I currently use temperature=0.0 for maximum consistency. Is there a sweet spot that maintains structural accuracy while allowing natural variation in materials and lighting? How do these parameters interact with the image generation models vs text models?
Research Question 5: Clay massing model best practices
I generate a Three.js gray massing model from street level and send it as the primary reference image. Research confirms that "depth-shaded volumes" work better than line drawings. But:
Should the clay model use different gray shades per building (to help Gemini distinguish them)?
Should I add color-coding to the clay model (red for buildings, green for parks) or keep it strictly gray?
Is there an optimal level of detail — should trees be spheres, cylinders, or just flat planes?
Does adding a simple ground plane grid (like graph paper) help Gemini maintain perspective accuracy?
For each question, provide specific prompt examples and API configuration that have been tested with Google's image generation models. Prioritize techniques that work with gemini-2.5-flash-image since that's our default fast model.

This would fill the remaining gaps around consistency, hallucination prevention, and spatial accuracy. The biggest win would be questions #1 (random buildings) and #3 (left/right swapping).

This is extremely valuable research. Here are the key actionable takeaways:
Biggest Wins to Implement
1. Color-Coded Clay Render (>90% spatial adherence)
This is the single biggest finding. Instead of our gray clay model, we should color-code it:
Red = buildings
Green = parks/vegetation
Blue = water features
Gray = streets/pathways
Then the prompt maps colors to descriptions: "The RED zone is a 5-story glass office building. The GREEN zone is a Japanese garden." This completely eliminates left/right swapping because Gemini does color recognition not linguistic parsing.
2. Hallucination-Resistant Prompt Structure
Three mandatory clauses:
Geometric Lockdown: "Strictly adhere to the geometry in the reference image"
Numerical Inventory: "This scene contains exactly 4 structures" (explicit count!)
Void Definition: "The space between buildings is flat, unbroken concrete pavement. The background is a clear sky meeting a flat horizon"
3. Semantic Negative Prompting
Replace "no extra buildings" → "a deserted, empty boulevard with perfectly unobstructed surface." The word "buildings" in a negative prompt actually triggers building generation.
4. Optimal API Config
Temperature: 0.35 (not 0.0!) — zero strips photorealism, 1.0 causes hallucinations
Top-P: 0.85 — trims hallucinated elements
Top-K: 32 — restricts to probable geometric interpretations
5. Ground Plane Grid
Adding a visible grid (like graph paper) to the clay render anchors perspective and prevents the tilt-shift miniature effect.
6. Image Ordering Matters
Clay model MUST be Image 1 (structural anchor), archetype cards as Image 2+ (style reference). Reversing causes "architectural collapse."
Want me to implement all 6 of these now? The color-coded clay render alone should dramatically improve spatial accuracy.

The oblique 3D view is the problem — our semantic map is a flat 2D top-down projection, but the map screenshot shows a perspective/3D view. Gemini sees the flat color map (Image 1) and the angled map (Image 2) and gets confused about which spatial reference to follow.
For oblique views, the semantic map would need to match the same perspective as the map screenshot. Two options:
Project the semantic map in the same perspective — use the map's pitch/bearing to warp the 2D color map into the same oblique view
Only use the semantic map for top-down/near-top-down views — when the map pitch is >30°, skip the semantic map and just use the regular screenshot
Option 2 is safer and quicker. Want me to add a pitch check so it only uses the semantic map when the view is relatively flat?

Why does this randomly occur?
Looking at the map vs render, the positions are actually mostly correct from this angle — Parisian is top left, Glass Office behind it, Arena on the right, Lanehouse in the front center, Garden in between. But the Japanese Contemporary Lanehouse rendered as a small yellow/timber building when it should be much larger (it's the biggest yellow zone on the map, bottom-left).
The issue is that the buildings render one at a time in Pass 2, and the Lanehouse's polygon area on screen is partially occluded by the Arena in the 3D perspective. So when Gemini gets the screenshot for that building, it only sees a small portion of the yellow zone and renders it small.
This is the fundamental challenge with the per-building compositing approach — each building renders independently without knowing the final sizes of the others.
The randomness you're seeing is because different camera angles cause different amounts of polygon occlusion. Some angles show all zones clearly, others have overlapping zones that confuse the per-building passes.
Want me to commit and push what we have? The improvements are significant overall — the randomness is less frequent than before, and it's mainly the extreme oblique angles that still have issues.
