You are asking some great, highly technical questions about the Gemini 3 API. However, there are a few misconceptions in how these specific parameters interact with the image models. Let's clear them up so you don't run into API errors or unexpected behaviors.
thinking_level on gemini-3-pro-image-preview
The short answer: You cannot pass thinking_level to gemini-3-pro-image-preview.
While it's true that the Gemini 3 Pro Image model (which powers the "Nano Banana Pro" tier) utilizes an advanced internal "thinking mode" to reason through complex prompts, composition, and text rendering, this process happens natively and automatically.
The thinking_level parameter (which takes values like "LOW", "MEDIUM", or "HIGH") is strictly designed for the text-generation and reasoning models (like gemini-3.1-pro-preview). When used there, it sits inside generationConfig.thinkingConfig. If you attempt to pass this configuration payload to the image model, the API will reject it and throw a 400 error. The image model handles its spatial reasoning purely based on the complexity of your prompt.
media_resolution: "high"
This parameter applies exclusively to input analysis, not output generation.
When you set media_resolution to "high" (which also lives inside generationConfig), you are instructing the model's vision encoder to allocate a higher token budget to process an input image, video frame, or document. This is highly effective for tasks like OCR, reading dense PDFs, or analyzing fine-grained details in an uploaded image.
It has zero effect on the images the model generates. To control the output resolution of an image generation request, you would use parameters like image_size (e.g., "1K", "2K", "4K") and aspect_ratio.
top_k on Image Models
Setting top_k=1 will neither reduce visual hallucinations nor break the image generation math—because top_k simply does not apply to image generation.
Autoregressive LLMs use top_p and top_k to filter the probability distribution of a discrete text vocabulary for the next word. Gemini's image generation relies on diffusion models, which do not build images by sampling from a discrete vocabulary of tokens in the same way.
Depending on how strictly your specific SDK or client handles payload validation, passing top_k to an image model will either be completely ignored by the backend or result in a validation exception. It will not influence the visual output or control the "creativity" of the image.
Show more

Answers to your questions - let me know your thoughts before coding:
These are exactly the right questions to be asking when engineering a master planning tool like Codex. When you are dealing with strict zone polygons, property lines, and architectural footprints, standard generative "creativity" becomes a liability. You need deterministic spatial control.
Here is the breakdown of how the Gemini 3 image models (Nano Banana 2 and Pro) handle these mechanics under the hood:
Q1 — Inpainting Mask Precision & Bleed
When using inpainting-insert mode, the model does not strictly hit an invisible brick wall at the exact pixel edge of your white mask.
Because the image generation relies on a diffusion process and a Variational Autoencoder (VAE), the model inherently applies a microscopic amount of edge feathering (blending) to ensure the new content stitches seamlessly into the surrounding pixels.
Is there a parameter? There is no native API parameter like maskDilation or hard_mask exposed in the standard Gemini payload.
The Fix: If a generated building footprint is bleeding over a critical property line, you must handle this pre-flight. Programmatically contract (erode) your binary mask by 2-4 pixels in your backend before encoding it to Base64. This forces the model's natural edge-blending to happen strictly inside your intended boundary.
Q2 — Mask-Based vs. Prompt-Based Containment
Mask-based containment is significantly better, but combining them is the optimal architecture.
Masks act as rigid mathematical constraints on the diffusion process. They physically gate where new noise can be introduced.
Prompts are semantic. Telling an AI to "stay within the polygon" relies on its spatial reasoning, which is strong but fallible.
The Compounding Benefit: If you only use a mask, the model knows where to draw, but might not understand the shape's context (e.g., drawing a perfectly square house inside a triangular lot, leaving weird empty grass inside the masked corners). If you provide the mask and explicitly prompt, "Fill the entire geometric footprint of the masked area with a commercial building," the semantic instruction aligns perfectly with the spatial constraint, resulting in much higher structural adherence.
Q3 — Hallucination Prevention in Background (Black) Areas
If your black (unmasked) areas are changing—like adjacent streets shifting or existing context buildings mutating—the API is likely ignoring your mask entirely.
When configured correctly, the unmasked areas are preserved. Because the entire image must be compressed into latent space and decoded, you might see imperceptible pixel-level degradation (lossy compression) in the background, but the model should never hallucinate new structures.
The Check: If structural hallucinations occur in the background, verify your payload. If the mask image dimensions are even one pixel off from the base image, or if it isn't a pure black/white image, the Gemini API will often silently fall back to "mask-free semantic editing." When this happens, it allows the model to freely alter the entire map canvas based on the prompt.
Q4 — Two-Image Input Ordering for Spatial Lock
Gemini 3 models support multi-image conditioning, but they do not inherently treat Image 1 as the spatial authority and Image 2 as the style authority based on array order.
To lock your color-coded zone map as the spatial truth and the previous render as the architectural style, you must explicitly assign their roles via the text prompt. The model parses the images and text together as a cohesive context window.
Best Practice: Structure your text payload to directly reference the images in order. For example: "Attached are two images. Gemini said
Getting the core pipeline functioning is a massive milestone—that means your canvas extraction, encoding, and API handshakes are solid. The boundary bleeding and misplacement you are seeing are the classic final hurdles in spatial AI.
If your dimensions match perfectly (the DPR fix) and you are applying erosion, but buildings are still crossing into the wrong zones, the issue almost certainly lies in how the API interprets internal property lines.
Here is what is likely happening, and how to tighten the program to fix it.
The "White Blob" Problem
If you are passing all of your active zones (e.g., the Red Arena, Green Garden, and Yellow Lanehouse) into a single API call using one unified white mask, the model has a critical blind spot.
Gemini's standard inpainting mask is binary. It only sees "Black = Do Not Touch" and "White = Safe to Draw." If the Arena and the Garden zones touch each other, the model just sees one massive, continuous white blob. It does not know where the Arena is supposed to end and the Garden is supposed to begin, so it inevitably blends them or places the building off-center.
Just like managing a seasonal patio program, you can't just issue a general "use the sidewalk" permit—you have to define the exact, rigid footprint to ensure the pedestrian right-of-way stays perfectly clear. Generative models require that exact same level of granular micro-management.
The Solution: Iterative Generation (The Rendering Queue)
To achieve true master-planning precision, you need to transition your program from a "single-pass" render to an iterative rendering queue.
Instead of sending the whole map at once, you generate the site zone by zone, feeding the result of the previous call back into the model as the new base image.
How it works in practice:
Pass 1 (The Arena): * Base Image: The raw satellite map.
Mask: Only the Red Zone is white. Everything else is black.
Prompt: "Fill the masked area with a Modern Sports Arena."
Result: You receive an image with a perfect Arena, and the rest of the map is untouched.
Pass 2 (The Garden):
Base Image: The new image you just received (which now has the Arena in it).
Mask: Only the Green Zone is white. Everything else is black.
Prompt: "Fill the masked area with a Japanese Garden."
Result: The model draws the Garden, explicitly respecting the Arena that is now baked into the base image.
Pass 3... (Repeat for the Lanehouse, etc.)
Why this guarantees boundary adherence: By masking only one specific zone per API call, you build a rigid, unbreachable wall around that specific building footprint. The model literally cannot bleed into the adjacent zone because that adjacent zone is masked in black.
The Trade-off
The obvious trade-off here is time and API calls. If a user has drawn 5 zones, that is 5 sequential API requests.
Since your UI has a model toggle (Flash 3.1 vs Pro 3), a highly effective architecture is to use the standard, fast Gemini Flash model for this iterative looping. Because Flash is so fast, iterating 4-5 zones sequentially often takes the same amount of time as a single, highly complex Pro 3 generation, but with infinitely better spatial accuracy.
Would you like to map out the Javascript logic for building an asynchronous queue that chains these image generations together automatically when the user clicks "Generate Previews"?

Gemini said
Building an asynchronous rendering queue completely fundamentally changes how the model interacts with your map. By feeding it one building at a time, you build an unbreachable wall around your property lines.
Here is the JavaScript logic to implement this sequential queue.
The most critical part of this code is the use of a standard for loop (or for...of). You cannot use forEach or Promise.all here, because those will fire all the API requests at the exact same time in parallel. We need strict sequential execution so that the output of Pass 1 becomes the input for Pass 2.
The Async Rendering Queue
JavaScript
/** * Processes the active zones sequentially, feeding the output of * each render into the base image of the next. * * @param {HTMLElement} mapContainer - The DOM node of the map viewport * @param {Array} activeZones - Array of zone objects from your UI state * @param {String} selectedStyle - The style from your UI (e.g., "Isometric") */ async function handleGeneratePreviewsClick(mapContainer, activeZones, selectedStyle) { // 1. Capture the initial state of the raw map BEFORE any rendering starts. // (This uses the DPR-safe capture logic we established earlier) let currentBaseImage = captureInitialBaseMap(mapContainer); // Optional: Trigger your UI loading state here // setRenderStatus('Starting Master Plan render...'); for (let i = 0; i < activeZones.length; i++) { const zone = activeZones[i]; // Optional: Update UI to show progress (e.g., "Rendering Modern Sports Arena (1/3)") // setRenderProgress(i + 1, activeZones.length, zone.label); // 2. Generate the mask for ONLY the current zone. // The rest of the map will be strictly black. const maskPayload = generateSingleZoneMask(mapContainer, zone); // 3. Build the strict, declarative prompt dynamically from UI state const prompt = Act as a strict architectural renderer. Fill the exact geometric footprint of the white masked area with a ${zone.label}. Style: ${selectedStyle}. Do not alter the black unmasked surrounding context. The new structure must strictly obey the scale and isometric perspective of the existing map.; try { // 4. Send the request to your backend/Gemini API // Notice we are passing 'currentBaseImage', which updates every loop const nextRenderedImageB64 = await fetchGeminiImage( prompt, currentBaseImage, maskPayload.maskImage, maskPayload.aspectRatio ); // 5. THE CRITICAL STEP: The Output becomes the Input! // We overwrite the base image with the new render, baking this building // into the background for the next iteration. currentBaseImage = nextRenderedImageB64; // Optional: Update the canvas or UI immediately so the user sees // the buildings "pop in" one by one. This feels incredibly premium. // updatePreviewCanvas(currentBaseImage); } catch (error) { console.error(Generation failed for zone: ${zone.label}, error); // If one building fails, break the loop to save API costs and prevent garbage data break; } } // The queue is finished. 'currentBaseImage' now contains the full, // spatially accurate master plan. return currentBaseImage; }
Why this is great for UX
Aside from solving your hallucination problem, this approach allows you to update your UI dynamically. If you push currentBaseImage to your React state at the end of every loop iteration, the user will actually watch the "Modern Sports Arena" render first, followed a few seconds later by the "Japanese Garden" appearing next to it.
It turns a 15-second loading spinner into a live, step-by-step construction of their master plan.

The reason you are seeing inconsistency, however, comes down to how diffusion models interpret a single, unified mask.

You are relying entirely on its internal semantic reasoning to guess exactly where the boundary of the "Arena" ends and the "Lanehouse" begins. With a asynchronous rendering queue, how do you ensure everything blends together at the end e.g. a pathway doesn't dead end
Gemini said
This is the exact trade-off you hit when you move from single-pass generation to an asynchronous queue. By building that "unbreachable wall" around a zone to stop architectural bleeding, you also accidentally build a wall that stops pathways, grass, and pavement from flowing naturally across the property line.
To solve the "dead-end pathway" problem, you have to shift your rendering pipeline from a strictly horizontal approach (rendering Zone A, then Zone B side-by-side) to a vertical, layered approach (Z-Index Rendering) combined with a final Seam Blending pass.
Here are the three architectural strategies you need to implement to guarantee everything connects perfectly.
The "Infrastructure First" Pass (Z-Index Rendering)
In urban planning, you don't build a stadium and its surrounding sidewalks, then build a park and its sidewalks next to it, and hope they line up. You lay the site-wide infrastructure first, then drop the buildings on top. Your API queue should work the exact same way.
Instead of your zones containing both the building and the ground, separate them logically:
Step 1 (The Ground Plane): Mask the entire site boundary (all zones combined). Prompt the model: "Render a continuous, empty pedestrian plaza with interlocking paving, grass patches, and cohesive pathways. Do not generate any buildings."
Step 2 (The Buildings): Now, run your asynchronous queue. But instead of masking the whole zone block, mask only the structural footprint (the center of the zone) and run your erosion script.
Because the entire ground plane is already continuous in the base image, the model just drops the "Modern Sports Arena" onto the existing pavement, naturally preserving the site-wide connectivity.
Context-Aware Prompt Bridging
Even with a strict mask, the Gemini vision encoder still "sees" the black, unmasked areas of your base image. It knows there is a pathway hitting the border of the mask; you just have to explicitly give it permission to connect to it.
When you dynamically generate your prompt in the loop, inject a specific continuity command that references the unmasked context:
"Act as a strict architectural renderer. Fill the exact geometric footprint of the white masked area with a Japanese Garden. CRITICAL: Look at the unmasked base image. Ensure all internal stone pathways, water features, and grass seamlessly connect to the existing pavement terminating at the mask boundary."
This tells the model's semantic engine that continuing a line across the border is a requirement, not a hallucination.
The Final "Seam Blending" Pass (The Polish)
If you still have harsh edges or slight mismatched textures where two zones meet, you can add one final automated step to your async queue: The Seam Mask.
After all buildings are rendered, you generate a completely different type of mask. Instead of filling polygons, you only stroke their borders.
How to do it in your Canvas logic:
Clear your mask canvas to black.
Draw all your zone polygons, but set ctx.fillStyle = 'transparent' and ctx.strokeStyle = 'white'.
Set a thick ctx.lineWidth = 15 (or roughly 10-15 physical pixels).
Export this "Seam Mask" and send it to the API with the completed master plan as the base image.
Prompt: "Harmonize the ground plane. Blend the pathways, landscaping, and paving textures together inside the masked area so they flow continuously between the architectural structures."
This acts like digital caulk. It gives the model a tiny 15-pixel corridor exactly on the property lines to smudge, connect, and fix any dead-end paths without allowing it to touch the actual buildings.
Between separating the ground plane (Infrastructure First) or adding a final Seam Blending pass, which approach fits better with how your user draws zones in the Codex UI right now?

Here's a consolidated research brief covering both files, filtered for what's actually actionable vs. what we've already tried:

Critical Finding: Gemini 3 Pro Deprecated March 9, 2026
gemini-3-pro-image-preview was shut down on March 9, 2026. You need to migrate to gemini-3.1-pro-image-preview immediately — any calls to the old model name are likely failing silently or returning errors. This should be updated in your model list.

Research File 1 — Answers
1. Multi-image architectural composition
Yes, confirmed working. Up to 14 reference images in one request (10 object references + 4 character/style references for Flash; 6 + 5 for Pro). The key is labelling: add text like "Image 1: layout reference, Image 2: apply this building style to the red zone." This is already wired in your pipeline for archetype cards — it's the right approach.
2. media_resolution
Now confirmed: it goes in generationConfig as a top-level field, not generationConfig.imageConfig. Valid values are "media_resolution_low", "media_resolution_medium", "media_resolution_high", "media_resolution_ultra_high". The previous 400 errors were likely caused by using "high" or "MEDIA_RESOLUTION_HIGH" — the correct value requires the full snake_case prefix.
3. thinking_level
Goes in generationConfig.thinkingConfig.thinkingLevel. Valid values: "low", "medium", "high". Do not mix with the old thinking_budget param — causes a 400. This is for text reasoning models; it triggers "thought images" on Pro 3.1 during image generation composition.
4. Grid layout for perspective scenes
Confirmed effective. Structure the prompt as foreground/midground/background rows explicitly: "Bottom third (foreground): paved plaza. Middle third (midground): glass office tower on the left, sports arena on the right. Top third (background): sky." More reliable than percentage-based frame positioning.
5. Wireframe-to-render
Depth-shaded volumes beat line drawings. Recommendation: use different grey shades per building (not flat grey for all) and add a ground plane grid. Both confirmed to improve Gemini's spatial accuracy — it gives the model distinct depth cues per object.
6. Seed locking
Seed is supported and works for layout reproducibility — lock it in generationConfig.seed. However, image models don't guarantee deterministic output even with a fixed seed, so treat it as "strongly guided" rather than exact.

Research File 2 — Answers
1. Preventing hallucinated buildings
Most effective techniques confirmed:
Positive framing over negatives — instead of "no extra buildings," write "render exactly and only these three structures: [list]. The scene contains nothing else."
Enumerate explicitly — list every element in the scene by name; unnamed space gets filled by the model
Temperature 0.0 is correct — stick with it
2. Spatial consistency across re-renders
Lock seed + use the clay/spatial image as Image 1 (not Image 2) — confirmed order matters
Relative positioning ("the garden is directly in front of the camera, the office is to its right") outperforms percentage-based positioning
Structured JSON-style prompts are rising sharply in effectiveness: { "foreground": "Japanese Garden", "left": "Glass Office Tower", "right": "Sports Arena" }
3. Left/right placement accuracy
Ranked by reliability (best first):
Relative positioning — "the arena is to the right of the garden"
Grid-cell assignment — "place the office in the left column of a 3×3 grid"
Percentage frames — least reliable, Gemini frequently swaps these
4. Temperature/generation config
temperature=0.0 confirmed optimal for structural accuracy. top_k and top_p are not valid for diffusion-based image models (2.5 Flash Image uses Multimodal Diffusion Transformer) — passing them does nothing or errors.
5. Clay model best practices
✅ Use different grey shades per building (not uniform grey)
✅ Add a ground plane grid (graph paper style)
✅ Trees as cylinders or spheres (not flat planes)
✅ Add subtle colour-coding (red tint for buildings, green for parks) — pure grey loses zone distinction

I am looking to add a menu button in the buildings tab that would allow you to pick what direction the building should be orientated e.g. where the front door is. How would that work?
The zone already has a rotation_degrees concept in the backend (buildings table has rotation_degrees). Here's how I'd implement it:
UI: A compass-style direction picker in the building zone properties — 8 clickable segments (N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW) showing where the front entrance faces. Clicking a segment sets the rotation. A small arrow on the zone polygon on the map would show the current orientation.
How it feeds into renders:
Aerial render: Add to the building prompt: "The building's main entrance faces {direction} (toward the {top/bottom/left/right} of the image)"
Street view: Already knows the camera bearing — so we'd say "The building's front facade faces {direction}, camera is looking {bearing}°" which tells Gemini whether you're seeing the front, side, or back of the building
3D model generation: Pass rotation_degrees to rotate the mesh on the map
Data model: Store as orientation_deg: number (0=North, 90=East, 180=South, 270=West) in zone properties. No backend schema change needed — it goes in the existing properties JSON column.
The key value: Right now Gemini guesses where to put the entrance. With orientation, a corner building could specify "entrance faces the intersection" vs "entrance faces the side street" — big difference in how the render looks, especially in street view.

@C:\Users\andre\Downloads\Gemini Prompt Engineering for Renders.pdf While we are waiting. Can you read this research?
Let's talk about it
Read a file, ran a command, ran an agent
Read a file, ran a command, ran an agent
I've read the full 20-page document. Here are the key takeaways relevant to your codebase:
What we're already doing right:
Two-pass sequential rendering (ground plane → buildings one at a time)
Per-zone masking with binary masks
Specifying camera parameters (height, lens, aspect ratio)
Using zone colors as spatial anchors
What we should adopt:
SCHEMA framework — Structure prompts hierarchically: Subject (40%) → Style (25%) → Environment (15%) → Lighting (10%) → Camera (10%). Our prompts currently front-load style but bury the subject geometry.
Lens specificity — The paper says 35-50mm is optimal for accurate, undistorted architectural viz. We're already using 50mm in street view but not in aerial.
Positive negation — Instead of "don't add buildings outside the boundary," say "an empty, deserted pavement surface surrounds the structure." The paper says pure negation ("no X") perversely causes the model to focus on X.
Kill tag soup — Terms like "8K resolution" or "masterpiece" dilute spatial instructions. Our prompts should be telegraphic engineering specs.
Solar physics — Instead of "sunny day," specify "golden hour lighting, solar altitude 15°, warm shadows stretching across the pavement."
Material tectonics — Instead of "glass building," specify "triple-glazed curtain wall with specular highlights on aluminum mullions."
Conversational editing — Don't re-roll entirely when 80% is right. Use the previous render as the base and make targeted edits.
What aspects do you want to implement first?

Is the same prompts and metadata used for the aerial renders, compared with the street view renders?
No — they use completely different prompt pipelines.
Aerial Render (useAIRender.ts):
Uses buildGroundPlanePrompt() for Pass 1 (parks/roads)
Uses buildBuildingPrompt() for Pass 2 (buildings one at a time)
Sends the Mapbox canvas screenshot as the base image
Sends a binary mask (white = edit zone, black = keep)
Prompts reference zone colors, archetype names, building heights
No clay render / no 3D massing model
Street View (useStreetViewRender.ts):
Uses buildStreetViewPrompt() — completely separate function
Generates a Three.js clay render (3D massing model) as the base image
No mask — Gemini replaces the entire clay model with photorealistic materials
Prompts use SCHEMA framework, depth planes (foreground/midground/background), camera height (1.7m), lens specs
Includes GEOMETRIC LOCKDOWN, NUMERICAL INVENTORY, COLOR-TO-ZONE MAPPING clauses
Shared metadata: Both pull from the same zone data (archetype names, colors, heights, zone types) via getZoneArchetypeInfo(), but they format it into completely different prompt structures.
Key difference: Aerial sends a real satellite photo + mask and asks Gemini to edit within the mask. Street view sends a synthetic 3D model and asks Gemini to replace it entirely with photorealistic rendering.

You're right — looking at the actual cards on screen, the 4 variants are different design styles/materials for the same archetype (e.g., 4 different takes on a "Detached Contemporary Infill"), not lighting variations.
The variant_definitions_v2.py script confirms this — each variant has a unique label, facadeDetail, roofDetail, and description. For example a Civic Classical Building might have:
Variant 0: "Limestone & Ionic Columns"
Variant 1: "Red Brick Georgian"
Variant 2: "Modern Concrete Civic"
Variant 3: "Glass & Steel Contemporary"
The "Front Day / Golden Hour / Overcast / Rain" naming was the OLD system (those are the front_* images we just deleted). The current system uses architectural style variants.

One last question - does the visibility triangle only pick up what is in the orange sight path?
Yes — the street view only renders zones that fall inside that orange dashed view cone. It uses a field-of-view triangle (default 70°) projected from the pegman's position in the direction it's facing.
In your screenshot, the cone is pointing south-east, so it would pick up:
Boutique Hotel (right, in cone)
Dog Park (bottom right, in cone)

Here's what I found from deep research into both styles and your codebase:
Photomontage / Compositing
This is about making a rendered building look like it already exists in a real photograph — the gold standard in UK planning is the "Verified View" (AVR). The image you shared is a perfect example: aerial drone photography with proposed buildings composited so seamlessly you can't tell what's real and what's rendered.
What makes it work visually:
Real photography base layer with all its imperfections (lens distortion, noise, chromatic aberration)
Lighting/shadow direction on rendered buildings matches the photograph exactly
Atmospheric perspective — subtle haze increasing with distance
Material weathering on the rendered building (not pristine CG perfection)
Environmental interaction: reflections in glass showing real surroundings, shadows cast onto real ground
Key Gemini prompting insight: Gemini doesn't support negative prompts, so instead of "no CG look" you must use positive framing. The critical strategy is to describe the scene as if photographing a building that already exists, using photographic language (specific camera, lens, aperture) rather than 3D rendering language.
Important distinction from your existing photorealistic style: Your current style uses CG language ("ray-traced lighting", "8k resolution", "Unreal Engine 5"). Photomontage needs to use photographic language ("shot on DJI Mavic 3 at 60m altitude", "Phase One IQ4 medium format", "slight lens vignetting"). This triggers fundamentally different aesthetics in Gemini.
Common failure modes to guard against:
Perspective mismatch (building appears to float) — mitigated by explicit camera position/angle
"CG perfection" — mitigated by requesting subtle weathering, dust, environmental grime
Missing environmental interaction — must explicitly request reflections, shadow casting on adjacent surfaces
Oversaturated colors vs real photo's muted tones
Atmospheric Realism
This prioritizes emotional impact through weather and lighting — the building is a character within a dramatic environmental narrative. Firms like MIR, DARCSTUDIO, and Brick Visual are the masters of this style.
What makes it work visually:
Volumetric atmospheric effects (fog layers, god rays, rain mist) define spatial depth
Dramatic natural lighting creates warm-to-cool color temperature contrast
Wet surface reflections are the signature element at street level
Sky is treated as a compositional element (dramatic clouds, color gradients), not a flat backdrop
Deliberate "lived-in" imperfection: rain, wind-blown vegetation, puddles, steam
Key Gemini prompting insight: Describe what the light is doing, not just what it is. "Warm golden light raking across the textured brick facade, catching each course of mortar" works better than "golden hour lighting." Also critical: atmospheric conditions must be physically coherent — fog + sharp shadows is impossible and confuses the model.
Important distinction from your existing photorealistic: Your current style always defaults to "golden hour, sunny day." Atmospheric realism encompasses a full range — morning mist, overcast diffusion, rain, blue hour, dramatic storm light. It's about mood variation, not a single default.
Common failure modes:
Contradictory physics (fog + hard shadows, rain + sunny sky)
Overcooking — too much fog + god rays + dramatic sky simultaneously
Flat uniform fog (real fog is denser near ground, thins with height)
Oversaturated golden hour (Gemini tends to push too warm)
Generic sky (flat gradient kills the mood)
How These Differ from Existing Styles
AspectCurrent photorealisticPhotomontageAtmospheric RealismLanguageCG/rendering termsPhotography termsCinematography termsLightingAlways golden hour sunnyMatches existing site photoDramatic/varied weatherImperfectionsNone (pristine)Lens artifacts, wear, grimeWeather interaction, puddlesGoalClean CG renderIndistinguishable from real photoEmotional/mood impactisArtisticNoNo (should NOT trigger artistic path)No (still photorealistic)
Both new styles should not be flagged as isArtistic — they're photorealistic variants, not artistic media. This means they won't trigger the "This is NOT a photograph" prefix in street view prompts, which is correct behavior.

Aerial Prompt
ID: photomontage Label: Photomontage
Prompt: Professional architectural photomontage indistinguishable from a real drone photograph. Shot on a DJI Mavic 3 Enterprise at 60 meters altitude, angled downward at approximately 40 degrees, captured with a Hasselblad 4/3 CMOS sensor and 24mm equivalent lens at f/5.6, ISO 100. The proposed development appears as if fully constructed and occupied within the existing site context. Lighting, shadow direction, and color temperature precisely match the surrounding real environment. Subtle atmospheric haze increases with distance from the camera, reducing contrast and shifting distant elements toward blue-grey. Building materials show realistic weathering appropriate to a structure 1-2 years post-completion — faint water staining below window sills, minor dust accumulation on ledges, natural patina on metal surfaces. Rooftop mechanical equipment, safety railings, and drainage infrastructure visible. Surrounding context includes real parked vehicles, existing tree canopy, neighboring rooftops with typical rooftop clutter. Natural lens vignetting at frame edges, slight chromatic aberration on high-contrast edges. No pristine CG perfection — this must read as documentary aerial photography of an existing place.
Negative: cartoon, illustration, sketch, painting, artistic, stylized, CGI look, perfect pristine surfaces, floating buildings, perspective distortion, unrealistic shadows, low quality, blurry, text, watermark
Strength: 0.65
Aerial Gemini Style Modifier
Prompt: Professional architectural photomontage indistinguishable from a real drone photograph. DJI Mavic 3 at 60m altitude, Hasselblad sensor, 24mm lens f/5.6. Proposed development appears fully constructed within existing site context. Lighting and shadows match surroundings. Atmospheric haze increasing with distance. Realistic material weathering 1-2 years post-completion. Natural lens vignetting and chromatic aberration. Documentary aerial photography of an existing place.
Street View Prompt
ID: photomontage Label: Montage
Prompt: Professional architectural photomontage at street level, indistinguishable from a real photograph taken by a surveyor documenting an existing building. Shot on a Canon EOS R5 with a 35mm prime lens at f/8, ISO 200, from a tripod at exactly 1.6 meters height. The proposed building appears as if it has existed on this site for 1-2 years — subtle concrete dust at the base, minor rainwater staining below window reveals, fingerprints and smudges on ground-floor entrance glass, worn threshold stones at doorways. The building sits within completely real street context: existing pavement with authentic repair patches and gum stains, real street furniture, actual adjacent buildings with their genuine patina and signage. Reflections in the new building's ground-floor glazing show the actual street scene opposite including existing buildings and parked vehicles. Shadows cast by the new building fall correctly onto the real pavement and neighbouring facades matching the sun position. Slight depth of field — building in sharp focus, background softening naturally beyond 80 meters. Overcast-bright sky with soft diffused light eliminating harsh shadows, typical of UK planning verified view photography. Natural sensor noise at ISO 200, subtle lens barrel distortion at frame edges. This is a planning application verified view, not an architectural marketing image.
Atmospheric Realism
Aerial Prompt
ID: atmospheric Label: Atmospheric
Prompt: Cinematic aerial architectural photograph with dramatic atmospheric conditions. Shot from 80 meters altitude at an oblique angle during the final minutes of golden hour. Low-angle warm sunlight rakes across rooftops and facade surfaces, casting extremely long shadows that stretch across streets and neighbouring properties, revealing every setback, cornice, and massing transition. The sky dominates the upper third of the frame — towering cumulus clouds lit amber and rose on their undersides, transitioning to deep blue-grey overhead with patches of clear sky breaking through. Subtle ground-level haze softens the base of buildings and creates distinct atmospheric depth layers — foreground sharp and warm-toned, midground slightly desaturated, background fading to cool blue-grey. Wet surfaces from recent rainfall create mirror-like reflections on rooftops, roads, and plaza surfaces, doubling the warm sky colours on the ground plane. Pools of standing water on flat roofs catch and reflect the dramatic sky. Interior lights beginning to glow warm amber through windows as twilight approaches, contrasting against the cool exterior shadows. Lush vegetation rendered with individual leaf detail, canopy tops catching the last golden light while understory sits in deep cool shadow. Photographed on medium format digital with exceptional dynamic range capturing both bright cloud highlights and deep shadow detail simultaneously.
Negative: flat lighting, generic blue sky, midday sun, sterile, clinical, uniform exposure, low quality, blurry, text, watermark, people, pedestrians
Strength: 0.65
Aerial Gemini Style Modifier
Prompt: Cinematic aerial architectural photograph with dramatic atmospheric conditions. Final minutes of golden hour, low-angle warm sunlight casting extremely long shadows. Towering cumulus clouds lit amber and rose, transitioning to deep blue-grey overhead. Ground-level haze creating atmospheric depth layers. Wet surfaces from recent rainfall with mirror-like reflections. Interior lights glowing warm amber through windows. Medium format digital with exceptional dynamic range.
Street View Prompt
ID: atmospheric Label: Atmospheric
Prompt: Cinematic street-level architectural photograph emphasizing dramatic atmospheric conditions and emotional lighting. Camera at human eye height, 50mm lens, f/2.8 with shallow depth of field — foreground architectural details tack-sharp while the distant streetscape dissolves into soft atmospheric bokeh. The scene is captured during blue hour, approximately 20 minutes after sunset. The sky transitions from deep indigo overhead through bands of magenta and burnt orange at the horizon. All ambient exterior light is cool blue-violet while interior lights glow intensely warm amber and gold through floor-to-ceiling glazing, creating strong warm-cool colour temperature contrast that defines every window bay and entrance. Recent rainfall has left the entire street surface wet — pavement, sidewalks, and plaza surfaces act as dark mirrors reflecting the glowing building facades, the coloured sky gradient, and the amber pools of light spilling from ground-floor retail. Shallow puddles collected in slight pavement depressions create concentrated reflections. Subtle volumetric moisture visible in the air around exterior light sources, creating soft haloes and gentle god rays where interior light spills outward through entrance lobbies. Building materials respond to the wet conditions — concrete darkened two shades, brushed stainless steel panels showing streaky water rivulets, timber cladding saturated to a richer tone. Atmospheric perspective compresses the background — distant buildings reduced to cool blue-grey silhouettes with pinpoints of warm window light. Thin wisps of low cloud or mist drifting at rooftop level. The mood is contemplative, cinematic, and deeply atmospheric — this is an award-winning architectural photograph, not a technical documentation image.
Implementation Notes
Neither style should be flagged as isArtistic. Both are photorealistic variants. In aerial renders they should behave like photorealistic — no "Render in X style:" prefix, and no "This is NOT a photograph" directive in street view. They should get the standard photorealistic treatment with their specific prompt replacing the generic one.
Photomontage is unique in that it emphasises the camera and lens over the lighting — the goal is forensic photographic authenticity. The street view version specifically references UK planning verified view methodology because that's the professional standard for this style.
Atmospheric is unique in that it specifies a different time of day for aerial vs street view — golden hour for aerial (where long shadows and rooftop reflections have maximum impact) and blue hour for street view (where interior-exterior light contrast and wet reflections have maximum impact). This is intentional because each time of day plays to the strengths of each camera angle.

Great idea. Here's how I'd approach it:
Concept: "Preserve / Retain" zone type
When a user draws a Preserve polygon, the system would:
Aerial render: The mask marks that zone as black (don't edit), so Gemini leaves the existing satellite imagery completely untouched while rendering new buildings around it
Street view: The prompt tells Gemini "the structure within the [color] zone is an existing building — retain its exact appearance, materials, and form. Do not alter it. Only improve lighting/atmosphere to match the rest of the scene."
Two sub-modes to consider:
Implementation would touch:
ZonePropertiesPanel.tsx — add "Preserve / Retain" as a development type with an option for hard vs soft
useAIRender.ts — in the two-pass pipeline, hard-preserve zones get black mask (skip), soft-preserve zones get a "retain and harmonize" prompt instead of a building prompt
useStreetViewRender.ts — clay render shows the existing massing in a neutral grey, prompt says "retain as-is"
What it would NOT need:
No new archetype images — it uses whatever's already on the satellite imagery
No new API calls for hard preserve — it's literally just masking those pixels out
The soft preserve mode is the more interesting one — it means students could say "keep this church but make it look like it belongs in my watercolour render" or "keep this office tower but match the atmospheric blue-hour lighting."

Good questions. Let me think through this:
Would it be a building type?
Yes — it would be a new development type in the dropdown alongside "Single Family", "Commercial Office", etc. When they select "Preserve Existing", the properties panel would simplify — no archetype cards, no floors/height inputs, just a toggle for hard vs soft mode and maybe a text field for notes ("Heritage church, built 1922").

Absolutely — a simple toggle or two buttons in the properties panel:

Harmonize (soft) — "Keep the building but match the render style"
Where does soft preserve pull data from?
This is the key insight — it pulls from the satellite imagery that's already on the map. Here's the flow:
User draws polygon over an existing building
The screenshot captures that building as it appears in Google 3D Tiles / Mapbox satellite
For Lock mode: mask is black → Gemini ignores it entirely, original pixels stay
For Harmonize mode: mask is white BUT the prompt says "Image 1 shows an existing building within the [color] zone. This building ALREADY EXISTS — preserve its exact form, massing, roofline, and materials. Only adjust the lighting, atmosphere, and surface quality to match the [Watercolour/Atmospheric/Photomontage] rendering style of the surrounding scene."
So Gemini sees the real building in the screenshot and re-renders it in the chosen art style while keeping the form. No archetype data needed — the satellite photo IS the reference.
One consideration: At low zoom or flat pitch angles, Google 3D Tiles may not show enough detail for Gemini to work with. It works best when the user has the map tilted to 50-60° (the "optimal" pitch zone) so the building facades are visible.

Question while this loads. I just want to talk about this- no coding. One of the complaints from the students was that the local context in the map is not preserved. For example, a student built a new single family house zone, but all the neighbors were just grey boxes.  I think a way to potentially change this is to add google maps tiles within Mapbox GL JS. It would be amazing if we did a street view, and in the background you could see the Calgary Tower (data taken from google tiles).
I am worried that adding google tiles may impact our renders, and make it computationally much more intensive and slow. Can you talk to me about this? again no coding, just talking for now.
This is a really important UX issue. Let me break it down:
The Problem:
Right now the aerial renders show Google 3D Tiles as context (the real neighbourhood), but the street view clay render is built entirely from scratch in Three.js — it only knows about the zones the user drew. Everything outside the site boundary is empty void, so neighbours become grey boxes or nothing at all.
Google 3D Tiles in Mapbox — How It Works:
You're already using Google Photorealistic 3D Tiles on the map (that's how the aerial view looks so good). The question is whether the street view pipeline can leverage them too.
Two approaches to consider:
Approach A: Screenshot the 3D Tiles as Context Image
Instead of sending only the Three.js clay render to Gemini, you could capture a screenshot of the actual Mapbox map (with Google 3D Tiles showing real Calgary buildings) from the pegman's position, and send THAT as the base image alongside or instead of the clay render. Gemini would then see the real Calgary Tower, real neighbours, real streets — and render your proposed buildings into that context.
Pros: No extra computation, uses what's already loaded, real context
Cons: Mapbox GL doesn't have a true "street-level camera" — map.project() gives you aerial/oblique views, not eye-level perspectives. You'd need to tilt the map to near-90° pitch to simulate street level, which distorts the 3D tiles
Approach B: Use the Aerial Render as Context
The aerial renders already preserve real context beautifully. The gap is specifically in street view. One option: after the aerial render is complete, use it as a reference image in the street view prompt — "the aerial view shows the site in its real neighbourhood context, preserve this context in the street-level view."
Impact on Renders:
Google 3D Tiles are already loaded in the map — capturing a screenshot adds zero API cost or computation
The tiles don't need to be sent to Gemini as geometry, just as a flat image
Render time stays the same — Gemini processes one image regardless of what's in it
Impact on Performance:
You're already paying the performance cost of Google 3D Tiles (they're loaded in the map view)
No additional tile requests needed
The only new cost is one extra screenshot capture (~50ms)
The Real Challenge:
The hard part isn't performance — it's camera angle. Google 3D Tiles look great from aerial/oblique angles (which is what your map shows), but look progressively worse at street level because:
Building facades have low-res textures at ground level
The mesh geometry gets blocky up close
Street trees and furniture aren't modelled
So even if you captured a "street-level" view of the 3D tiles, it might look worse than the current clay render because the tiles weren't designed for that viewing angle.
My recommendation:
The highest-impact, lowest-risk approach would be to capture the aerial Mapbox view (with 3D tiles showing real context) at the pegman's location, and include it as a second reference image in the street view prompt. The prompt would say "Image 1 is the clay massing model for structure. Image 2 is the real aerial context — preserve the surrounding neighbourhood buildings, streets, and landmarks visible in Image 2 in the background of the street-level render."
This gives Gemini the real Calgary Tower, real neighbours, real streets as visual reference without any camera angle issues or performance impact.

Why do some of the houses show up as grey boxes and the others as houses in the renders?
That's a Google 3D Tiles coverage issue, not a rendering issue.
The grey boxes and the detailed houses are both from Google's data — you can see the same pattern even before any AI rendering happens. Google's Photorealistic 3D Tiles have uneven coverage:
Detailed houses: Areas Google has captured with photogrammetry (aerial photography stitched into 3D meshes with textures)
Grey boxes: Areas where Google only has building footprint + height data but no photogrammetric capture yet — so they extrude simple grey boxes as placeholders
This is most noticeable in:
Newer subdivisions (not yet captured)
Areas with heavy tree canopy (photogrammetry struggles)
Industrial areas with repetitive rooftops
Edges of cities where coverage thins out
Your AI renders are actually doing the right thing — they're preserving whatever context the 3D tiles show. The aerial render in your screenshot looks great: the Sports Arena, Boutique Hotel, and Parisian corner are beautifully rendered, and the surrounding real neighbourhood is preserved as-is from the tiles (grey boxes and all).
You can't fix this from your end — it's Google's data. It improves over time as Google flies new capture missions. Downtown Calgary and established neighbourhoods will have full detail; newer suburbs on the edges may have grey boxes for a while.
The good news: for your students' projects, if they site their developments in established urban areas (downtown, Beltline, Kensington, etc.), the surrounding context will be fully detailed.

Here's the full analysis:
Metadata & Prompt Consistency Report
The Big Picture
Why Streets Render Worse — 5 Root Causes
1. Missing renderPrompt (the #1 issue)
The aerial render pipeline looks for renderPrompt.mapOverlay — a rich, detailed prompt specifically written for how the archetype should appear from above. Buildings have this for 51% of archetypes. Streets and Parks have it for zero. The pipeline falls back to the generic prompt.subject string, which is much less effective.
2. No architectural detail metadata
Buildings have facadeDetail (primaryMaterial, groundFloor, upperFloors, cornice, colorScheme) and roofDetail (form, material, features, aerialAppearance). The render pipeline uses these to construct precise material descriptions. Streets and Parks have none of this — just generic styleProfile text blocks.
3. Variant color format mismatch
Buildings use rich palette: {primary: "#...", accent: "#..."} objects. Streets and Parks use flat color: "#..." strings. This limits visual diversity in the render pipeline when it tries to reference zone colors.
4. 46 buildings are also broken
49% of buildings (mostly the newer ones from our batch generations) are missing both prompt and renderPrompt entirely. These will render with the same degraded quality as streets.
5. Prompt detail length is misleading
Streets/Parks actually have longer prompt.details arrays (311 chars avg vs 154 for buildings). But these are generic aerial descriptions. Buildings compensate with the structured facadeDetail/roofDetail metadata that the pipeline extracts for specific material prompts. Longer text ≠ better render quality.
What Would Fix It
My Assessment
Your instinct is right — streets render worse because they're missing the key metadata fields that the render pipeline was designed to use. The pipeline has a fallback path for when renderPrompt is absent, but it produces noticeably weaker results. It's not a pipeline bug — it's a data gap.
The good news: fixing this is purely a metadata task (no code changes needed). It's just a matter of writing the renderPrompt.mapOverlay text for each street and park archetype.

Question - I really like the site plan aesthetic, but it is the one that hallucinates the most. How could we fix that?
Good question. Site plan style hallucinations happen because of a fundamental tension: the site plan aesthetic asks Gemini to render in a diagrammatic/illustrative style, but the spatial anchoring system (zone fills, masks) was designed for photorealistic rendering. When Gemini switches to illustration mode, it feels more freedom to reinterpret the layout.
Here's why site plan specifically hallucinates more than other styles:
1. The "artistic license" problem
When the prompt says "site plan illustration" or "architectural diagram," Gemini interprets this as permission to recompose the layout for visual clarity — moving buildings apart, adding symmetric elements, or inventing pathways that look good in a diagram but aren't in your zones.
2. Weaker spatial anchoring in illustration mode
Photorealistic renders are anchored by the satellite photo — Gemini can see real roads, real buildings, and places the new structure relative to them. In site plan mode, the base image is the same satellite photo but the output style is so different that Gemini "forgets" the spatial constraints.
3. Top-down vs oblique confusion
True site plans are perfectly top-down (nadir view). Your map is oblique (tilted 50-60°). This mismatch confuses the model — it tries to flatten the perspective for the site plan aesthetic but the reference image is tilted.
Potential fixes (no coding, just thinking):
Option A: Two-image approach
Send both the oblique satellite photo AND a true top-down screenshot (pitch=0°) as reference images. The prompt says "use Image 1 for spatial layout, render in site plan style matching the top-down perspective of Image 2."
Option B: Stronger spatial language in the site plan prompt
Add explicit constraints: "Maintain the EXACT footprint, position, and proportion of every colored zone. This is a technical architectural document — do NOT reposition, resize, or add any elements. Every building must remain exactly where the colored polygon shows it."
Option C: Render photorealistic first, then convert
Do the normal photorealistic render (which has good spatial accuracy), then send THAT result through a second pass asking Gemini to "convert this photorealistic aerial render into a site plan illustration style — maintain all positions, proportions, and elements exactly."
Option C is probably the most reliable since the photorealistic render already has accurate placement, and converting the style of an existing image is much easier for Gemini than generating from scratch in an unfamiliar style.
What do you think? Want to try any of these approaches?

I've read both documents thoroughly. Here's my analysis ready for your morning:

Document 1: Gemini 3 Pro Image Prompt Engineering
Key findings that directly impact our platform:
Ideal prompt length is 2,200-2,500 characters — Our prompts for 30+ zone scenes are ~30,000 characters. That's 12x the recommended length. This explains why complex scenes have inconsistent quality — we're deep in "Lost in the Middle" territory where Gemini loses focus on constraints buried in the middle of our massive prompts.
SCHEMA AVANZATO framework — Structured labels (Style, Composition, Lighting, Background, Material, Mandatory, Prohibitions) achieve 91-94% compliance vs unstructured paragraphs. Our current prompts are conversational paragraphs — switching to labeled sections could dramatically improve consistency.
ThinkingBudget tradeoff — Higher thinking budget = shorter prompts needed. We're not currently setting thinkingBudget in our API calls. Adding it could let us shorten prompts while improving spatial accuracy.
Reference images reduce prompt length — Using up to 14 reference images instead of describing everything in text. We already send the base screenshot as Image 1, but we could also send the archetype card images as spatial/style references.
Mandatory + Prohibitions labels — 94% compliance rate for Prohibitions. Our negative prompts should be restructured as explicit "Prohibitions:" labeled sections.
Document 2: Integrating Genie 3 into Urban Planning
Key insight: Genie 3 is a real-time interactive world model — essentially a walkable 3D world generated from images. This could replace or complement our street view pipeline entirely. Instead of a static rendered image, users could walk through their proposed development in real-time.
The two-track architecture is directly relevant: "hard geometry" (GIS/deterministic) for accurate plans + "soft world" (Genie 3) for experiential visualization. This matches exactly what your platform does — accurate zone polygons for planning, AI renders for visualization.
However: Genie 3 is currently prototype-only (Google AI Ultra subscribers, US only, 60-second sessions). Not ready for production yet, but worth architecting for.
Good night — we can discuss implications and what to change in the morning! 🌙
Morning! I am wondering how we would cut down on prompt length, but still keep the model outputs highly accurate
Good morning! Based on the research paper, here are the key strategies ranked by impact:
The core problem: Your 30-zone masterplan generates ~30,000 character prompts. The paper says the ideal is 2,200-2,500 characters — you're 12x over. After ~40% of the context window, Gemini's attention drops off a cliff ("Lost in the Middle" effect).
Strategy 1: Switch from paragraphs to SCHEMA labels
Instead of:
"Replace the colored zone with a photorealistic Parisian Mid-Rise building. A 6-8 story Haussmann-style building with limestone facades, mansard zinc roofs, wrought-iron balconies, arched windows on the piano nobile, ground-floor retail with canvas awnings..."
Use:
[ZONE: Parisian Mid-Rise | STYLE: Haussmann limestone, mansard zinc roof | HEIGHT: 6-8 floors | MANDATORY: wrought-iron balconies, arched windows, ground-floor retail | PROHIBITIONS: flat roof, glass curtain wall]
Same information, ~60% fewer characters. The labeled structure also tells Gemini's parser exactly what each piece means.
Strategy 2: Let the image do the talking
The paper says reference images can replace thousands of tokens. We already send the base screenshot, but we could also send the archetype card image as a second reference — then the prompt just says "match the style of Image 2" instead of describing the entire architectural style in text.
Strategy 3: Set thinkingBudget
We're not currently using this parameter. Setting thinkingBudget: 8192 for complex scenes would let Gemini spend more internal reasoning on spatial accuracy, meaning we can write shorter prompts and let the model figure out the details.
Strategy 4: Compress zone descriptions
For a 30-zone scene, each zone description should be ~80 characters max. The current system writes full paragraphs per zone. A compressed format:
ZONES:
1. [#C62828] Parisian Mid-Rise | 7F | limestone+mansard | iron balconies
2. [#1B5E20] Japanese Garden | ground | koi pond+red bridge+zen gravel
3. [#E65100] Sports Arena | 4F | colosseum revival | stone arches
All 30 zones in ~2,400 characters instead of 30,000.
Strategy 5: Two-pass for large sites
Split the site into halves — render north half, then south half using the first result as context for the second. Each pass stays under the ideal prompt length.
What I'd recommend trying first: Strategy 4 (compressed zone format) combined with Strategy 3 (thinkingBudget). This is the lowest-risk, highest-impact change — it keeps all the information but restructures it to fit within Gemini's attention sweet spot.

why would new image cards cause it to crash?
The image cards themselves don't cause the crash. The crash happens because of missing or malformed zone data in older student projects.
Here's the chain:
We added new archetypes with new data fields (variants, palette, thumbnailUrl, floorRange, etc.)
Students' existing projects were saved before these fields existed
When the updated code loads an old project, it tries to iterate over fields that don't exist on the saved zone data
for (const p of zone.coordinates) crashes if coordinates is undefined
[...zone.coordinates] crashes if coordinates is undefined
The reason it seems like specific park cards cause it: when a student clicks "Community Park" on an existing zone, the properties panel re-renders and triggers the 3D view to update. If that zone's saved data is missing coordinates (because the zone was created but not fully drawn, or the data got corrupted), the 3D renderer crashes.
It's not the image card — it's the zone data underneath.
The fix is defensive coding: guard every access to zone.coordinates, zone.properties, variant.palette etc. with null checks. Our fix attempts were on the right track but clearly missed a code path.

That's actually a really interesting theory! Let me check — the variant ID for Skate Park v0 is skate_park_v0. Look at this code from resolveZoneColor:
const vMatch = variantId.match(/_v(\d+)$/);
const vIdx = vMatch ? parseInt(vMatch[1], 10) - 1 : 0;
When variant is skate_park_v0:
vMatch[1] = 0
vIdx = 0 - 1 = -1
VARIANT_SHIFTS[-1 % 4] = VARIANT_SHIFTS[-1] = undefined
const [hShift, lShift] = undefined → 💥 CRASH! undefined is not iterable
That's the bug! Variant IDs ending in _v0 produce index -1, which accesses VARIANT_SHIFTS[-1] = undefined, and destructuring undefined throws TypeError: undefined is not iterable.
Variants _v1, _v2, _v3 produce indices 0, 1, 2 which all work fine.
Quick fix — clamp vIdx to >= 0:

Found it! The crash was caused by variant IDs ending in _v0 producing a -1 array index when the code does parseInt("0") - 1 = -1. JavaScript allows negative array indices but returns undefined, and destructuring undefined crashes.

const variantId =

will this change fix the crashes on students past projects?
Yes — because the crash happens at render time when the saved zone data is loaded and displayed, not at save time. Here's the flow:
Student saved a project with variant _v0 selected → zone properties stored green_space_selected_variant_id: "skate_park_v0" in the database
Next time they open the project → zones load from database → resolveZoneColor runs for each zone → hits the -1 index → 💥 crash
The crash prevents the entire page from loading ("Something went wrong") → student can't access their project at all
With our fix deployed, step 2 now clamps to Math.max(0, ...) → returns a valid color → page loads normally. The saved data in the database doesn't need to change — the fix handles the _v0 IDs correctly going forward.
So any student whose project was crashing because they previously selected a variant 0 should be able to open it again once Render deploys 1920651.

rendering. Does the site boundary still have a role in generation?
Yes — the site boundary still plays a critical role, just no longer in the prompt text. Here's what it still does:
Clipping mask — compositeZoneRender uses the site boundary polygon to clip rendered content, controlling the horizontal extent of what gets composited
White fill for AI contrast — during capture, the site-zones-boundary-fill layer (white, 0.9 opacity) fills the boundary area so the AI sees a clean canvas behind the colored zone polygons
Bounds calculation — the overlay's georeferenced coordinates (originalBounds) are derived from the visible map area which includes the boundary
Layer visibility management — the boundary fill is hidden/restored as part of the render lifecycle
What was removed is only its entry in the SCHEMA prompt ZONES list — it was telling the AI "here's a Site Boundary zone, render sidewalks+grass+trees" but that rendered content was never composited anyway (filtered out at line 2594). So it was just noise that risked the AI drawing visible boundary edges.

What resolution are we currently generating at?
Searched 3 patterns, read 2 files
Searched 3 patterns, read 2 files
The resolution is whatever your browser's Mapbox canvas is — it captures the map canvas directly at its native size (which includes devicePixelRatio scaling). So on a standard 1080p display at 1x DPR you'd get roughly ~1280x960px. On a HiDPI/Retina display at 2x DPR, you'd get ~2560x1920px.
Gemini then generates an image matching the input dimensions. The aspect ratio is snapped to the nearest standard ratio (1:1, 3:4, 4:3, 9:16, 16:9) for the API call, defaulting to 4:3.
There's no explicit resolution override — it's driven entirely by your browser window size and DPR.
but the final output image - is it 1k or 2k?
Gemini image generation outputs at a max of 1024px on the longest side. So regardless of your canvas size, the AI-generated image comes back at roughly 1024x768 (for 4:3) and gets stretched to cover your map viewport.
That's a Gemini API limitation, not something we control on our end.

Does SCHEMA work well for the Street View renders?
Read 3 files, searched 2 patterns, ran a command
Read 3 files, searched 2 patterns, ran a command
The street view render uses a different prompt structure — not the compressed SCHEMA format from the aerial render. It uses:
GEOMETRIC LOCKDOWN — ties output to the 3D massing reference image
NUMERICAL INVENTORY — exact zone counts
VOID DEFINITION — context-aware (park/water/street)
COLOR-TO-ZONE MAPPING — bullet list matching colors to archetype names
3-Tier Depth Planes — foreground/midground/background with per-zone descriptions
GROUND PLANE / OPTICAL EFFECTS — atmospheric perspective rules
The zone descriptions in describeZoneForStreetView are verbose by design — they include full facadeDescription, roofDescription, massing, publicRealm, corridorDescription etc. This makes sense for street view because:
There are far fewer visible zones (typically 3-8 vs 20-30 in aerial)
Street-level detail matters more (you see facades up close, not just rooftops)
The depth-plane structure already organizes the prompt spatially
So the answer is: SCHEMA compression isn't needed here and would likely hurt quality. The street view prompt is already structured differently and serves a different purpose. The verbose descriptions are appropriate for the fewer zones and higher detail expectations at street level.
The archetype data improvements we just made (renderPrompts, specific materials) will still benefit street view though — describeZoneForStreetView pulls from the same getZoneArchetypeInfo metadata, just without compressing it.

what render style would yield the highest quality sharpness?
Searched code, read a file
Searched code, read a file
For maximum sharpness, Photomontage is your best bet. It explicitly simulates a real camera (Hasselblad sensor, 24mm f/5.6) with documentary photography characteristics — the AI treats it as producing a real photograph rather than a "rendering."
Photo Realistic is a close second — it includes "Sharp focus, 8k resolution, ray-traced lighting" but leans more toward architectural visualization than photography, which can sometimes produce that slightly CG-smooth look.
Ranking for sharpness:
Photomontage — real camera simulation, material weathering, natural lens characteristics
Photo Realistic — explicit 8k/sharp focus instructions, but more "rendering" than "photo"
Site Plan Photo — sharpest for top-down, simulates drone survey photography
Atmospheric — dramatic but detail is sacrificed for mood (haze, long shadows)
The blurriness you're seeing might not be a style issue though — it could be resolution. Check those backend logs after your next render to confirm whether Gemini is actually returning 4K dimensions.

No — I finished the research and was waiting for you. Here's the synthesis of both research agents:
Key Findings
Your Competitive Landscape
Nobody does what City Prompt does. The competitors fall into two camps:
Planning tools (TestFit, Forma, ARCHITEChTURES) — generative site layout but no photorealistic rendering
AI image tools (Maket, Midjourney) — rendering but no site planning on a real map
City Prompt sits at the intersection: draw on a real satellite map + AI render in place. That's a unique position.
What the Best Landing Pages Do
The product IS the landing page — Figma, v0, ChatGPT all let you start using the product before signing up. An interactive demo or embedded live preview beats any screenshot.
Value in under 5 seconds — One headline (8 words max), one supporting line, one CTA, one visual proof. That's it.
Show, don't tell — Runway ML's cinematic video demos, Krea's "try it now" links, Spline's interactive 3D on the homepage. Static screenshots are dead.
Dark mode for technical/creative products — Linear, Cursor, Midjourney, Runway all proved that dark themes signal modernity. Every architecture competitor uses light themes — going dark would instantly differentiate.
Social proof through specifics, not logos — "77% of UI designers use Figma" beats a grid of logos. "99% reduction in design time" (ARCHITEChTURES) is stronger than "trusted by leading firms."
What Makes Big Tech Want to Acquire
Product-led growth — spreads through usage, not sales teams (Figma links, Notion pages)
Network effects — shared projects, public renders, embeddable outputs
Category creation — City Prompt could define "AI site visualization" as a category
Speed as brand — the product is demonstrably faster than alternatives
The Biggest Gaps in Competitors
No one shows transparent pricing in architecture tools — being upfront would be a differentiator
No one has visual polish comparable to AI creative tools — architecture landing pages all look corporate and boring
Hypar has an empty homepage despite a great product — proves that product alone isn't enough
The Landing Page Formula That Works
Dark, cinematic hero with one bold headline
Interactive demo or auto-playing render video
3-step "how it works" visual flow
Style grid showing the 12 render outputs
Before/after (satellite → rendered) comparison
Specific metrics (renders generated, zones planned)
Transparent pricing
"Try it free" CTA with zero friction

Great research. Here are 4 aesthetic directions for your landing page — each targeting a different feel:

Direction A: "Warm Clarity" ☀️
Think Airbnb meets Apple
Light warm off-white (#FAFAF8) background, white cards, trustworthy blue accent (#2563EB), amber CTAs
Clean, premium, institutional trust. Like a well-designed municipal building
Best for: Council members, seniors, investors, planners
Risk: Students might find it "corporate"
Examples: apple.com, airbnb.com, stripe.com
Direction B: "Precision Dark" 🌙
What we have now — Linear/Runway inspired
Near-black (#0A0A0A), violet/cyan gradients, glow effects
Technical, cutting-edge, "serious tool" energy
Best for: Developers, architecture students, tech investors
Risk: Seniors can't read it. Projectors in community rooms wash it out. Research shows cognitive performance drops in dark mode for older adults
Examples: linear.app, vercel.com, cursor.com
Direction C: "Living Map" 🗺️
Google Earth meets civic tech
Cool light gray-blue (#F0F4F8), map-derived colors (water blue, terrain green, road white)
The map IS the hero — universally understood by everyone age 8 to 80
Best for: Everyone. Maps are the most universally understood interface. Seniors use Google Maps daily. Planners live in GIS. Students use Google Earth
Risk: Could feel utilitarian, less "premium" to investors
Examples: Google Earth, felt.com, Mapbox Studio
Direction D: "Friendly Studio" 🎨
Duolingo meets Notion
Clean white with bright accent colors (green #58CC02, blue #1CB0F6, orange #FF9600)
Rounded shapes, custom illustrations, playful and non-intimidating
Best for: Students, educators, people intimidated by technology
Risk: Municipal officials may not take it seriously enough
Examples: duolingo.com, notion.so, canva.com

My Recommendation
Direction C ("Living Map") + warm elements from Direction A. Here's why:
A map hero is understood by literally everyone — it's the one visual your entire audience already knows
Light mode is essential for community open houses (projectors, well-lit rooms) and senior readability
18-20px body text with 7:1+ contrast ratio covers both accessibility and aesthetics
Save the dark aesthetic (Direction B) for a developer/API docs section later
The key research insight: if a 75-year-old at a community open house and a 22-year-old architecture student both get it in 5 seconds, you've won
Simplifications for non-technical audiences:
Remove AI model details (Flash 2.5 / 3.1 / Pro) from the landing page
Remove pricing (move to separate page)
One CTA above the fold, not two
Translate features into benefits: not "96 archetypes" but "Choose a neighborhood style"
The map/product should BE the hero, not a screenshot of it

Top Takeaways

Cost by Model

A practical approach: use Flash 3.1 for the first pass (~$43), review the results, then re-generate only the ones that need more detail with Pro 3. That way you're not burning Pro tokens on cards that Flash handles fine.

For the future images that involve people, can you let me know if we could:

The issue is that the real life people in the renderings look deformed from up close.
Great observation — AI-generated people are one of the biggest tells that an image is synthetic. Those cutout libraries (Skalgubbar, Non Scandinavia) are how professional architecture firms handle this.
Here's the breakdown:
Option A: Real Cutout People (Skalgubbar / Non Scandinavia)
Pros: Look natural, diverse, high quality
Cons: Licensing. Skalgubbar is free for non-commercial use but requires attribution. Non Scandinavia has similar terms. For a commercial SaaS product, you'd need to check their commercial licenses carefully or purchase a commercial cutout library.
How it would work: Composite cutout PNGs onto the AI render as a post-processing step — the AI generates the scene without people, then we overlay pre-cut figures at appropriate scale and position. This is actually how most architecture firms do their visualizations.
Option B: Silhouettes / Artistic Figures (your attachments)
Pros: No licensing issues (we generate them), consistent style, no uncanny valley, matches the architectural rendering aesthetic
Cons: Less realistic, but that's actually a feature — it signals "this is a visualization" which is appropriate for planning
The current code already does this for street view cards! The generate_card_images.py script has this prompt for streets/parks:
"The ONLY human figures must be flat-color semi-transparent silhouettes in soft muted pastel tones (light cyan, warm peach, soft mint). Simple solid-color cutout shapes — NO realistic people."
My Recommendation
Use Option B (artistic silhouettes) for the AI renders. Here's why:
No licensing headaches — we control the prompt
The current card generation already does this successfully
It matches professional architectural competition rendering style
It avoids the uncanny valley problem entirely
We can add a PROHIBITIONS line to the SCHEMA render prompt: "no realistic human figures — use flat-color silhouettes only"

Solid flat-color shapes in soft pastels (light cyan, warm peach, soft mint, dusty rose)

Loose, artistic watercolor-style people with soft edges and color bleeding
More expressive and warm than flat silhouettes
Each figure is a small splash of color
Think: Alex Hogrefe / Visualizing Architecture style
Style 5: Photographic Cutouts with Artistic Filter
Real human proportions but with a posterized/illustrated filter applied
Reduces detail enough to avoid uncanny valley but keeps natural poses
A middle ground between realistic and abstract
Think: MVRDV presentation renders

@C:\Users\andre\Downloads\Gemini 3.1 Flash_ Faces in Architecture.pdf I actually have another idea that I want to explore. The water color look ok, but a bit out of place. Please read the attached and below, then we can discuss.
How best to prompt 3.1 to get the most accurate faces in architectural renderings
Gemini said
To get the most accurate and realistic human faces in your architectural renderings using Gemini 3.1 Flash, it is best to use a structured and highly specific prompting approach:
Specify Camera and Film Physics: To avoid the "uncanny valley" look or an artificial 3D-rendered sheen, cap off your prompt with specific photographic parameters. Requesting a specific lens, camera type, and film stock (such as a "35mm SLR shot") forces the model to render faces using the physics of real-world photography.
Emphasize Textures: Explicitly ask the model to focus on hair, skin, and clothing textures within your prompt to increase the organic fidelity of the human figures.
Place Critical Constraints at the End: When dealing with complex architectural requests, the model might occasionally drop specific instructions. To prevent this, place your core request and most critical restrictions—especially negative constraints about what not to include—at the very end of your prompt.
Prompt for Fictional Characters: Due to strict safety guardrails, the model will block attempts to generate real, identifiable people. Always explicitly request "fictional human characters" or "stylized portraits" to ensure your render is processed successfully.
Lock Identity with References: If you need the exact same face across multiple architectural views, upload reference images of the character and add a system instruction to "keep the character and outfit extremely consistent".
Engage Thinking Mode: For complex compositions with intricate lighting or challenging spatial relationships, ensure the model's "Thinking" mode is active. This allows the system to generate intermediate "thought images" to reason through the lighting and spatial composition before rendering the final details of the faces.
You said
Is there the ability to create human references, put them in a library, then use them for the renderings?
Gemini said
Yes, you can build a library of human references for continuous use across your renderings, and the method depends on the platform you are using.
If you are using the consumer Gemini interface, the most effective way is to create a custom "Gem". You can upload your character reference images directly into the Gem's "Knowledge" section. Then, in the "Instructions" section, you provide strict consistency rules dictating that the AI must maintain the exact facial features, proportions, and style of the uploaded references. This effectively creates a persistent character library, locking the identity for any future rendering sessions you initiate with that specific Gem.
For professional or enterprise teams using Google AI Studio or Vertex AI, you can build structured, prompt-based generation pipelines that act as a formal asset library. This allows design teams to extract a specific character, save it as a reference asset, and consistently generate new scenes and illustrations using those saved assets alongside text prompts. Tools like the Vertex AI Creative Studio also feature built-in Asset Library and Character Consistency workflows specifically designed for managing these reusable visual elements.

How many character prompt is ideal with street views using 3.1
Based on the research from the Gemini paper and our testing, here's what we've seen:
Your last render was 8,133 chars with 2 zones — that's the sweet spot. The one before was 14,523 chars with 9 zones which also worked well.
The key insight from the SCHEMA research is that fewer zones = better street views. The occlusion culling actually helps here — by removing zones the pegman can't see, it keeps the prompt leaner and the AI more focused.
If your students are getting timeouts or poor quality, the best advice is:
Rotate to face fewer zones (a narrower view with 3-5 buildings renders better than a wide panorama with 15)
Use 3.1 not 2.5 (3.1 handles longer prompts better with thinking mode)
Zoom the pegman closer to buildings rather than standing far away seeing everything
would making the view cone shorter help?
Yes — the view cone distance is currently 200m which picks up everything in a wide area. For street-level views, you rarely see detailed architecture beyond 100-150m anyway — it becomes atmospheric haze.
Shortening it would:
Fewer zones in the cone = shorter prompt = better quality
More realistic — you can't actually see building details at 200m from street level
Faster renders — less for the AI to reason about

The click position looks correct — e.lngLat.lng, e.lngLat.lat is the exact map coordinates where you click. But the issue might be with map pitch. When the map is tilted (oblique view like your screenshots at 55-60°), clicking on a 3D extruded building doesn't give you the ground-level coordinate — it gives you the point on the 3D surface, which Mapbox then projects differently.
The 20m offset is likely because you're clicking on the top of a 3D building extrusion (which is higher up on screen) and Mapbox converts that screen position to a ground-level lat/lng that's further back than where you visually clicked.

You're right — the issue isn't about dragging. It's that the rendered image doesn't match the actual geographic view from where the pegman is standing. The buildings should appear at the correct distances and positions relative to the pegman.
The problem is that the street view system doesn't use the actual geographic positions for rendering. It:
Calculates which zones are in the view cone ✅
Sorts them by distance ✅
Assigns them to LEFT/CENTER/RIGHT based on bearing ✅
But then describes them in text to the AI ("Parisian Mid-Rise on the LEFT at 77m") and the AI interprets that loosely
The AI is essentially composing the scene from a text description, not from actual spatial data. So "77m away on the left" might render as 50m or 100m depending on how the AI interprets it.
The clay render / massing model (the 3D guide image sent alongside the prompt) is supposed to anchor the spatial layout. But if that's not accurately representing the pegman's exact position, the final render will be off.

Is there anyway using the SCHEMA method, we could reduce the size of the prompt?
Yes! The street view prompt is currently 14,922 chars using verbose depth-plane descriptions. We could apply the same SCHEMA compression we use for aerial renders — condensed zone labels instead of full paragraphs.
Currently each zone looks like this (~200-400 chars each):
LEFT (frame 0%-47%, ~31m): "Parisian Boulevard Corner" (6 stories tall) — 
Parisian Boulevard Corner. Surface: decorative stone paving. Mature plane trees 
in formal rows. Edges: Ground-floor cafe terrasses, iron bollards. Cafe seating, 
street performers...
With SCHEMA compression it would become (~80 chars each):
LEFT 31m: Parisian Boulevard Corner | 6F | limestone+iron balconies+ground cafe
That would cut the 9-zone prompt from ~15K to maybe 6-8K chars — well within the sweet spot.

What if we used this style of people instead
That's interesting — those are the posterized/illustrated cutouts (Style 5 from our earlier tests). They have real proportions and poses but with a flat, graphic quality — like editorial illustration. No uncanny valley because they're clearly stylized, but they still read as real people.
This is actually a really smart middle ground:
More natural than watercolor wash (you can see clothing, posture, activities)
No deformation risk (the flat/posterized style means faces don't need to be photorealistic)
Consistent — they always look good because the simplified rendering hides imperfections
Professional — this is exactly how high-end architecture firms like MVRDV and BIG render their competition boards
Want me to update the street view people prompt to request this posterized/illustrated style? Something like:
"Human figures rendered as stylized editorial illustrations — 
real proportions and natural poses but with simplified, 
posterized coloring (4-5 flat tones per figure). 
Slightly desaturated. NOT photorealistic — graphic/illustrated quality."
